policies.title: Informed Consent, Representatives and Decision-Making Support
policies.applies_to: All employees, the Administrator, the governing body, residents, representatives and prescribers who work with [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure residents take part in decisions about their own lives and care, that consent is obtained from the right person, and that no one with a conflict of interest acts as a resident's representative.
policies.policy: This policy meets 290-9-37-.07(3)(c) (How the residence guarantees the rights of residents) and 82-13-1-.05(8)(d) (proposed) (How the residence guarantees the rights of the residents as outlined in Section .15). [AGENCY NAME] guarantees each resident the right to take part in care planning, to choose a physician, to read the admission agreement or receive reasonable accommodation, and to see and copy his or her own records. A resident's representative may be a guardian, spouse, adult child, parent, attorney, adult next of kin or adult friend. No governing body member, staff member or family member of staff may serve as a resident's representative or guardian. Consent for psychotropic medication follows the capacity and informed consent process and the priority order in O.C.G.A. 31-9-2. Restraints and medical support devices require discussion with the resident and guardian and authorization in the ISP. A resident may report suspected abuse, neglect, exploitation or abandonment privately, even over the objection of a guardian.

definitions.definition: Agreement to a treatment, medication or device after being told in understandable terms what it is, why it is proposed, its risks and benefits, and the alternatives, including the option to refuse.
A guardian; spouse; adult child; parent; attorney; adult next of kin; or adult friend who acts for a resident.
The resident's ability to understand information, appreciate its effect on him or her, weigh options and communicate a choice, assessed for the specific decision at hand.
A medication prescribed to affect mood, thinking or behavior.
A device used for a medical reason to support a resident's body or function, as defined in the DBHDD proposed rules and addressed in RST-01.
As defined in the DBHDD proposed rules and in RST-01. Mechanical and chemical restraint and seclusion are never used on residents.

procedures: At admission, the Administrator asks the resident who the resident wants involved in decisions and records the name and relationship of any guardian or representative. The Administrator obtains a copy of any guardianship order or other legal document and files it in the resident's record.

The Administrator confirms that the representative is not a governing body member, a staff member or a family member of staff. If one is proposed, the Administrator refuses the arrangement in writing, informs the governing body, and helps the resident and family find another representative.

The Administrator presumes every adult resident can make decisions unless a court has ruled otherwise. A resident under guardianship still takes part in decisions in the manner and to the extent he or she is able.

Staff explain each decision to the resident in plain language, in his or her preferred communication method, at a pace the resident can follow, and allow time for questions (see RGT-05). Staff use pictures, simple words, interpreters or assistive technology when needed.

The ISP team, including the resident, invites the resident to every planning meeting. The resident's choices on goals, services, schedule, roommates and physician are written in the ISP in the resident's own words where possible (see PCS-01).

The Administrator reads the admission agreement aloud, or provides it in an accessible format, to any resident who cannot read it, and records the accommodation provided. Copies go to the resident and the representative (see ADS-01).

Before a new psychotropic medication or a dose change, the nurse or Administrator confirms with the prescriber that informed consent has been obtained and documented. The prescriber is asked to describe the medication, its purpose, risks, benefits and alternatives to the resident and the decision-maker.

The capacity and consent process for psychotropic medication follows the priority order in O.C.G.A. 31-9-2. The Administrator documents who gave consent, on what date, with what information, and the basis on which that person has authority to consent. The consent is filed in the resident's record.

If a resident has capacity, the resident consents for himself or herself. If the resident lacks capacity and has a guardian, the guardian consents within the scope of the guardianship order. If neither applies, the Administrator and the prescriber follow the O.C.G.A. 31-9-2 priority order and consult the DBHDD regional field office when the proper decision-maker is not clear.
Staff never give consent for a resident. If no authorized decision-maker can be identified, the Administrator notifies the DBHDD regional field office and documents the effort made.

A resident has the right to refuse any medication or treatment. Staff do not force, trick or coerce a resident to take medication. They document the refusal, notify the prescriber and the representative, and follow MED-01 and MED-03.

A restraint is never used as a substitute for treatment or support. Mechanical and chemical restraint and seclusion are never used. A medical support device may be used only after discussion with the resident and guardian, a prescriber's order where applicable, and authorization in the ISP (see RST-01 and RST-02).

Consent is reviewed at least annually at the ISP meeting, whenever the medication or device changes, and whenever the resident's capacity appears to have changed. The Administrator records each review.
Staff support the resident's right to choose his or her own physician. The Administrator records the physician choice and helps the resident arrange appointments and transport.

The resident may see and copy his or her own records on request. The Administrator provides access during business hours, or sooner when practical, and records each request and response (see REC-01 and CONF-01).

Staff post and review with each resident the right to report suspected abuse, neglect, exploitation or abandonment privately, even over a guardian's objection, and to complain to DBHDD. Staff give the resident private telephone access to do so and do not tell the representative or the Administrator what the resident said unless the resident agrees or law requires (see ABE-01 and RGT-02).

If a resident and a representative disagree, staff record both views, support the resident's voice, and ask the Administrator to convene the ISP team. The Administrator consults DBHDD where a concern about the representative's actions exists.

responsibilities.duty: Prohibits any governing body member, staff member or staff family member from serving as a representative or guardian and reviews compliance.
Verifies representatives, ensures consent is obtained and filed, arranges accommodations and maintains the records.
Confirms consent before psychotropic medication starts or changes and supports the prescriber's explanation to the resident.
Explain decisions in plain language, support resident choices and report concerns about consent or representatives.
Take part in planning and decisions and tell the agency of changes in representative or legal status.

Accommodation notes for reading the admission agreement
Physician choice record
Records access and copy log
Medication refusal notes

policies.title: Nondiscrimination and Communication Access
policies.applies_to: All employees, the Administrator, the governing body, residents and representatives of [AGENCY NAME]
federal: Title VI of the Civil Rights Act (42 USC 2000d)
policies.purpose: To make sure every resident receives services without discrimination and can understand and take part in the home's processes through language and communication supports.
policies.policy: This policy meets 290-9-37-.07(3)(c) (How the residence guarantees the rights of residents) and 82-13-1-.05(8)(d) (proposed) (How the residence guarantees the rights of the residents as outlined in Section .15). Nondiscriminatory services are a non-waivable right of every resident. [AGENCY NAME] does not discriminate in admission, services, discharge or treatment on the basis of race, color, national origin, language, disability, sex, religion, age or other protected status, consistent with the Americans with Disabilities Act and Title VI of the Civil Rights Act. The agency provides reasonable accommodation so residents can read or understand the admission agreement, and provides interpreters or accessible formats at admission, rights review and ISP meetings. Copies of agreements go to the resident and the guardian.

definitions.definition: A change in format, method or timing that lets a resident understand information and take part, without imposing an undue burden on the agency.
Information provided in a way the resident can use, such as large print, plain language, Braille, audio, pictures or electronic text.
A limited ability to read, speak, write or understand English.
A qualified person who conveys meaning between languages, including sign language, without adding opinion.

procedures: At the first contact and again at admission, the Administrator asks the resident and the representative about preferred language, how the resident communicates, and any hearing, vision, literacy or cognitive needs. The answers are written in the resident's record and the ISP.

The Administrator does not deny admission or retention, and does not treat residents differently, because of a protected characteristic or disability. Admission and retention decisions rest only on whether the home can meet the person's needs (see ADM-01).

Before the admission agreement is signed, the Administrator offers the resident the chance to read it. The Administrator reads it aloud, uses plain language, large print, pictures, an interpreter or other supports for any resident who needs them, and records the accommodation used on the agreement checklist.

The Administrator gives a copy of the signed admission agreement to the resident and the guardian, and records the date and method of delivery. Where the copy is not understandable to the resident, a version in an accessible format is also given.

The Administrator arranges a qualified interpreter or accessible format for admission, rights review, ISP meetings, grievance meetings and consent discussions, at no cost to the resident. Staff do not rely on other residents or on children to interpret, and use family members only when the resident asks for it and the Administrator agrees.

The Administrator keeps a current list of interpreter services, including spoken languages and sign language, and of sources for accessible formats, in the Administrator's office. The list is reviewed twice a year.

Staff learn each resident's communication method, such as speech, gestures, device, signs or pictures, from the ISP and use it. Assistive communication devices stay with the resident, are charged and are in working order.

The Administrator posts the DBHDD and regional field office telephone numbers and the rights summary in a place residents can reach, in the languages and formats used in the home. Staff review the rights with each resident on admission, annually and when asked.

Staff do not refuse service, offer a lower standard of service, or make disparaging remarks based on a protected characteristic or a resident's disability. A staff member who sees or suspects discrimination reports it to the Administrator the same day. A staff member may also report directly to DBHDD.

The Administrator investigates a discrimination complaint under RGT-02, tells the resident the outcome in an accessible format, and keeps the record. Retaliation against anyone who complains is prohibited.

Staff give residents the same choices on food, activities, visitors, bedroom, schedule and religion regardless of protected status, and respect residents' cultural, religious and personal preferences as recorded in the ISP (see PCS-01 and HLT-04).

If a request for accommodation cannot be met, the Administrator tells the resident and the representative in writing why, offers an alternative, and records the decision. The resident may appeal through RGT-02.
The Administrator reviews communication-access needs for each resident at each ISP meeting and whenever the resident's condition changes. Updates are recorded in the ISP.
All staff are trained on this policy at orientation and annually (see STF-04). The Administrator reviews requests for accommodation and complaints quarterly as part of QA (see QA-01).

responsibilities.duty: Adopts this policy, provides resources for interpreters and accessible formats, and reviews complaints.
Assesses communication needs, arranges accommodation, keeps the resource list, investigates complaints and keeps records.
Use each resident's communication method, report discrimination and support understanding in all interactions.
Tell the agency about communication needs and raise concerns about unequal treatment.

documentation: Communication and language needs assessment in the record and ISP
Admission agreement accommodation checklist
Record of delivery of agreement copies to resident and guardian
Interpreter and accessible-format request log
Resource list of interpreters and format vendors
Discrimination complaint investigations
Staff training sign-in sheets

policies.title: Medication Management and Supervision
policies.applies_to: All employees, the Administrator, nursing and pharmacy consultants, prescribers and residents of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure every resident receives medication safely, in the way that suits his or her ability, with all aspects of medication management documented.
policies.policy: This policy meets 290-9-37-.07(3)(d) (How the residence supervises medications) and 82-13-1-.05(8)(e) (proposed) (Procedures for all aspects of medication management including medication orders and procurement, storage, security, method(s) of administration used, documentation, and disposal of discontinued or out of date medications, as outlined in Section .14). [AGENCY NAME] uses one or more of four administration pathways for each resident: proxy caregiver, assisted self-administration, self-directed self-administration, or licensed professional. Every medication requires an order or prescription signed within the past year. Initial orders are procured within 24 hours and refills are obtained before the supply runs out. Only a physician or pharmacist may repackage or dispense medication. Medications are stored locked. A monthly Medication Administration Record (MAR) is kept for every method of administration. Only licensed persons administer medication, except as the proxy caregiver rules and the emergency medication rules permit.

definitions.definition: An unlicensed person who is trained and authorized under the DBHDD rules to administer medication to a resident who cannot self-administer, as defined in the proposed CLA rules.
The resident takes his or her own medication with staff help, such as reminders, opening containers or handing the medication to the resident.
The resident independently takes his or her own medication and staff only oversee.
A person licensed in Georgia to administer medication, such as a registered nurse or licensed practical nurse, who administers within his or her scope.
The Medication Administration Record, which records each medication given or not given, with the legend and signatures.
Right resident, right medication, right dose, right time, right route, right reason, right documentation and right to refuse.
A drug regulated under state or federal controlled-substance law, kept double-locked.

procedures: The Administrator and the nurse or other licensed professional determine the administration pathway for each resident under MED-02 before any medication is administered. The pathway is recorded in the ISP and the MAR.

Medication is given only on a written order or prescription signed by a prescriber within the past year. The Administrator or nurse checks that a signed order is on file for every medication, including over-the-counter products and supplements, before it is given. Orders unsigned or older than one year are renewed with the prescriber.

At admission or when a new medication is ordered, staff obtain the initial supply within 24 hours of the order. If this is not possible, staff notify the prescriber the same day and document the reason and the plan.

Staff request refills before the supply is exhausted, using a refill check at least [NUMBER OF DAYS] days before the last dose. Staff document the request. If a resident would run out, the nurse or Administrator contacts the prescriber and pharmacy and records the outcome.

Only a physician or pharmacist repackages or dispenses medication. Staff do not transfer medication between containers, pre-pour medication, or divide or crush medication unless a prescriber or pharmacist has ordered it. Medication stays in the pharmacy-labeled container with the resident's name, medication, dose, route, frequency, prescriber and date.
Staff check each new delivery against the order and the MAR before it is put away. Any difference is reported to the pharmacy and the nurse before the medication is given, and recorded.

Medications are stored in a locked cabinet or drawer, separated by resident. Refrigerated medications are kept in a locked container or locked refrigerator at 36-41°F with a daily temperature log. Controlled substances are double-locked and counted at each shift change by two staff (see MED-04).

Only authorized staff hold medication keys. The Administrator keeps a key log and changes access when staff leave. Keys are never left in a lock or handed to residents except as the ISP allows for self-directed residents.

A resident on assisted or self-directed self-administration keeps medications according to the capacity assessment. Where the ISP allows personal storage, the medication is in a locked space the resident can open, and staff check supplies and the MAR at the intervals set in the ISP.

Only staff authorized for the resident's pathway administer. A licensed professional administers where the resident's needs require it. A proxy caregiver administers only after training and competency testing as required by MED-04 and only under the rules for proxy caregivers, within the limits of the written order.

Staff follow the eight rights at every administration. They wash hands, check the MAR against the label, give the medication, watch the resident take it, and initial the MAR immediately. They never sign for a dose before it is given or for a dose given by someone else.

A MAR is kept every month for every resident and for every method of administration, including self-directed self-administration. The MAR lists the resident's name, allergies, diagnosis, medication, dose, route, time, prescriber, start and stop dates, a legend with initials and signatures, and codes for refusals, holds and omissions.

Staff document refusals, held doses, missed doses, PRN medications (with reason given and result) and any side effects. They notify the nurse or prescriber of repeated refusals or of any effect that concerns them.
The nurse or Administrator reviews each resident's MAR at least weekly and the whole medication record monthly, and signs the review. Findings go to QA (see QA-01).
Discontinued, expired or unused medications are removed from active storage, documented and disposed of as described in MED-04. Medications of a discharged resident are handled under ADS-04.
Medication errors, emergencies and allergies are handled under MED-03. Concerns about a resident's ability to self-administer are handled under MED-02.

A pharmacist or registered nurse independent of the agency completes a medication-management assessment at every site that houses medications at least every two years, and the Administrator corrects deficiencies within the time set in the report (see MED-02 and GOV-02).

responsibilities.duty: Adopts this policy and ensures resources for safe medication management.
Oversees the medication system, verifies orders, supervises staff and ensures the independent assessment is done.
Assesses residents, administers medication where required, trains and tests staff and reviews MARs.

responsibilities.role: Proxy caregivers and direct support staff
responsibilities.duty: Administer or assist only within their authority and training, document accurately and report problems immediately.
Write and dispense medication orders and give consultation.

Procurement and refill log
