policies.title: Determining Administration Method and Self-Administration Capacity
policies.applies_to: The Administrator, nurse or licensed professional, direct support staff, ISP team members, prescribers and residents of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To choose the safest and least restrictive method of medication administration for each resident, based on a documented assessment of capacity, and to act quickly when concerns arise.
policies.policy: This policy meets 82-13-1-.14(14) (proposed) (a written policy specifying procedures for oversight of medication), 82-13-1-.14(14)(a) (proposed) (processes for determining the methods of medication administration and the assessment of the resident's capacity to self-administer) and 82-13-1-.14(14)(b) (proposed) (actions to take when concerns about a resident's capacity to self-administer are identified). [AGENCY NAME] assesses each resident's capacity to self-administer before choosing an administration pathway, and records the result and the pathway in the ISP. The agency supports a resident in taking as much control of his or her medication as is safe. When concerns arise, the agency takes the written actions in this policy. The agency also carries out a polypharmacy review, an Abnormal Involuntary Movement Scale (AIMS) every 12 months where indicated, and a medication-management assessment by an independent pharmacist or registered nurse every two years at every site that houses medications.

definitions.definition: The resident's ability to identify his or her medications, know the purpose, dose and time, take them correctly, store them safely and report problems.
One of four methods of medication administration: proxy caregiver, assisted self-administration, self-directed self-administration or licensed professional.
A structured review of a resident's total medications by a prescriber, pharmacist or nurse for duplication, interactions, unnecessary medication and side effects.
The Abnormal Involuntary Movement Scale, a standard screening for movement disorders in residents taking certain psychotropic medications.
Any sign that a resident may not be safely managing his or her medications.

procedures: Before any medication is given or kept by a resident, the nurse or other licensed professional [NURSE NAME] completes a written self-administration capacity assessment. The Administrator ensures it is done before or at admission and before any medication is handled.

The assessment records whether the resident can name each medication and its purpose, state the dose, time and route, read the label or use an aid, open and take the medication, tell when a dose is missed, store the medication safely, refuse, and report side effects. It also records the resident's history, vision, dexterity, memory and communication.
The resident takes part in the assessment, and the representative and the prescriber are consulted. The resident's own wishes about managing his or her medication are recorded.

The nurse recommends a pathway: self-directed self-administration for a resident who manages independently; assisted self-administration for a resident who can take medication with help; a proxy caregiver or a licensed professional for a resident who cannot self-administer. The ISP team confirms the pathway and the Administrator records it in the ISP and on the MAR.
The least restrictive pathway that is safe is chosen. A resident is not placed on a more restrictive pathway because of staff convenience, and the reasons for any limit are written in the ISP.

A resident on assisted or self-directed self-administration has a written support plan stating what staff do, how often staff check supplies and the MAR, where medication is stored, and what signs mean the plan must be reviewed.

The assessment is repeated at least every 12 months, at each ISP review, after a hospitalization, after a medication change that affects ability or schedule, and whenever a concern is identified. Each reassessment is dated and signed.

Any staff member who has a concern about a resident's capacity, for example missed doses, taking the wrong medication, stockpiling, refusals, confusion, injuries or reports from the resident, tells the nurse or Administrator the same shift and writes an incident note.

When a concern is identified, the nurse or Administrator within 24 hours (a) checks the resident's safety and the medication supply and count; (b) notifies the prescriber if the resident has missed or taken doses wrongly; (c) increases staff checks or moves to a more supportive pathway on a temporary basis if needed for safety; and (d) informs the resident and the representative.

Within [NUMBER OF DAYS] days of the concern, the nurse repeats the capacity assessment, and the ISP team, including the resident, meets to decide whether to continue, add support or change the pathway. The reasons and the plan for returning to a less restrictive pathway are recorded.

If a resident disagrees with a change of pathway, the Administrator records the resident's view, explains the reasons, offers a review at the next ISP meeting, and tells the resident how to complain under RGT-02.

The nurse or pharmacist reviews each resident's medication list for polypharmacy at least every 12 months and whenever the list changes substantially, and records the findings and communication with the prescriber. The Administrator checks that each recommendation is acted on or answered.

For each resident taking medication that requires monitoring for movement disorders, the nurse or prescriber carries out an AIMS where indicated at least every 12 months, and the result and any follow-up are filed in the record.

The Administrator arranges for an independent pharmacist or registered nurse who is not an employee of the agency to carry out a medication-management assessment at every site that houses medications at least every two years. The Administrator corrects each finding by the date in the corrective action plan (see GOV-02) and keeps the report.
Staff who give or assist with medication are trained on the pathways and this policy at orientation and annually (see MED-04 and STF-04).
Results of capacity assessments, concerns and pathway changes are reviewed quarterly in QA (see QA-01).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures assessments are completed on time, pathways are recorded, concerns are acted on and the biennial assessment occurs.
Performs capacity assessments, polypharmacy reviews and reassessments, and advises the ISP team.
Choose the least restrictive safe pathway and review changes.
Observe, report concerns the same shift and follow the support plan.
Review the medication list, order or perform AIMS where indicated and respond to notifications.

documentation: Self-administration capacity assessments and reassessments
ISP entry of pathway and support plan
Concern reports and follow-up notes
Polypharmacy review records
AIMS results
Independent pharmacist or RN assessment reports and corrective action
Notification records to prescriber, representative and resident

policies.title: Medication Emergencies, Errors and Allergy Flagging
policies.applies_to: All employees who give, assist with or observe medication, the Administrator, the nurse, prescribers and residents of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure staff respond quickly to medication emergencies, define, document and report medication errors, and prevent harm by flagging allergies and other critical information.
policies.policy: This policy meets 82-13-1-.14(14)(c) (proposed) (emergency procedures: employees to be notified, local poison information center number, person responsible for decision making, and the physician, clinic or emergency room to be contacted), 82-13-1-.14(14)(e) (proposed) (definitions and procedures for documenting and reporting medication errors) and 82-13-1-.14(14)(f) (proposed) (procedures to flag allergies and other critical information). Staff call 911 for any life-threatening medication emergency. Non-licensed staff trained and authorized by [AGENCY NAME] may give emergency medications: epinephrine, seizure rescue medication, glucagon and naloxone. Every medication error is documented and reported, and the prescriber is notified. Allergies and other critical information are flagged on the MAR and in the record.

definitions.definition: A resident's condition that is life threatening or may cause serious harm due to a medication, such as overdose, severe allergic reaction, wrong medication taken, severe side effect, ingestion by the wrong person, or seizure, low blood sugar or opioid overdose needing rescue medication.

Any departure from the prescriber's order or the eight rights, including a wrong resident, medication, dose, time, route or reason; an omitted or extra dose; a dose given without a current order; an undocumented dose; medication given after expiration; or a dose given by someone not authorized.
An error caught before it reaches the resident.
Allergies, adverse drug reactions, swallowing or choking risks, medications that must not be crushed, high-alert medications, seizure or diabetes emergency plans, and do-not-use items.
Epinephrine, seizure rescue medication, glucagon and naloxone, which non-licensed staff may give when trained and authorized.

procedures: The Administrator posts a Medication Emergency Sheet next to each medication storage site and in the emergency binder. It lists the Administrator [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] [PHONE], the nurse [NURSE NAME] [PHONE], the on-call manager [PHONE], the Poison Help Line 1-800-222-1222 (the local poison information center), the person responsible for decision making for each resident (resident, guardian or representative), and the resident's physician, clinic, nearest emergency room [ADDRESS] and pharmacy. The Administrator checks it monthly.

In a medication emergency, the staff member present first calls 911 if the resident is unresponsive, has trouble breathing, has a seizure not ending as directed by the plan, has chest pain, severe swelling or hives, or is otherwise in danger. If the resident is conscious and stable, the staff member calls the Poison Help Line and follows its advice.

Non-licensed staff trained and authorized under MED-04 give emergency medications as ordered and as taught: epinephrine for anaphylaxis, seizure rescue medication for a seizure, glucagon for severe low blood sugar and naloxone for suspected opioid overdose. The staff member calls 911 at the same time or immediately afterward, stays with the resident and gives first aid until help arrives.

Staff keep the resident's medication list, allergy list, face sheet and the container of the medication involved, and give them to emergency personnel. A staff member goes with the resident or follows the ambulance when possible.

As soon as the emergency is under control, staff notify the Administrator, the nurse, the prescriber or clinic, and the person responsible for decision making. The Administrator then follows ABE-02 and HLT-03 for incident reporting and change of condition.
A medication error is any event within the definition above. Staff report any error or near miss to the nurse or Administrator immediately upon discovery, and never alter a record to hide one.

On discovering an error, the staff member checks the resident's condition, keeps the resident safe, and calls 911 or Poison Help if there is any sign of harm. The staff member does not give a dose to correct an error unless a prescriber or poison center instructs it.

The staff member or the nurse notifies the prescriber, or the clinic or on-call physician, right away, and follows their instructions. The Administrator notifies the guardian or representative the same day, and the resident is told in plain language what happened.

The staff member completes a Medication Error Report before the end of the shift stating the resident, medication, dose, time, what happened, who found it, the resident's condition, who was notified and what instructions were given. The Administrator reviews the report within 24 hours.

The Administrator decides whether the error is also a reportable incident under ABE-02 and REC-02. Errors that cause harm, require medical care or are associated with neglect are reported as required there.

The Administrator and nurse review each error within [NUMBER OF DAYS] days for cause, such as staffing, labeling, distractions or training. They put in place corrective action, which may include retraining or removal from medication duty, and record it. Staff are not penalized for reporting but may be retrained or disciplined for repeated or reckless errors.
Errors and near misses are counted and reviewed quarterly in QA (see QA-01).

At admission, the nurse or Administrator records each resident's allergies, including drug, food, latex and environmental allergies, with the reaction, and records "No Known Allergies" if none. The source is the resident, representative, prescriber or pharmacy.

Allergies and other critical information are flagged in red at the top of the MAR, on the face sheet, on the front of the record, in the emergency binder, and in the kitchen where food allergies apply. They go to the pharmacy and with the resident on every medical visit and transfer.

Staff check the allergy flag against each new order before giving the first dose. If a medication conflicts with a recorded allergy, staff do not give it and call the prescriber and pharmacist at once.

The nurse updates the flags within 24 hours of any new allergy, adverse reaction or critical information and informs all shifts by the shift communication log. The Administrator verifies the flags monthly.
Staff are trained on this policy at orientation and annually, including emergency medication use, and the Administrator keeps competency records (see MED-04 and STF-04).

responsibilities.duty: Maintains emergency sheets, ensures reporting, reviews errors, corrects causes and verifies allergy flags.
Advises on emergencies and errors, notifies prescribers, trains staff on emergency medications and updates critical information.
Respond to emergencies, give authorized emergency medications, report errors immediately and follow allergy flags.
Give instructions when notified of an error or emergency.
Is notified and takes part in decisions as decision maker.

documentation: Medication Emergency Sheet with poison center and contact numbers
Emergency medication orders and staff authorization records
Medication Error Reports and near-miss records
Notification records to prescriber, representative and Administrator
Corrective action and retraining notes
Allergy flags on MAR, face sheet, record and emergency binder
Monthly flag verification checklist
Incident reports where required

policies.title: Medication Storage, Disposal and Staff Medication Training
policies.applies_to: All direct support staff, the Responsible Staff Person, the Administrator, the Nurse/RN consultant, and any contractor who handles, administers or assists with medications at [AGENCY NAME] Community Living Arrangement sites.
policies.purpose: To keep every resident's medications secure, correctly stored, accounted for and properly disposed of, and to make sure only trained and competency-tested staff administer or assist with medications.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] stores all medications in locked storage, keeps refrigerated medications at 36-41F with daily temperature logs, and keeps controlled substances under double lock. Medications that are discontinued or out of date are removed from use immediately, held securely and disposed of by the documented procedure in this policy. Only staff who have been trained by a physician, physician extender, registered nurse or pharmacist, and who pass competency testing at least annually, may administer or assist with medications, and only under the administration pathway set for the resident in MED-01 and MED-02. Only a physician or pharmacist may repackage or dispense medication. This policy meets 82-13-1-.14(14)(d) (proposed), procedures regarding management of medications including disposal of discontinued or out-of-date medications, and 82-13-1-.14(14)(g) (proposed), requirements for staff training. It is written to the proposed Chapter 82-13-1 and will be updated if the final adopted rule differs.

definitions.definition: A medication scheduled under state or federal law (for example, certain opioids, benzodiazepines and stimulants) that requires double-locked storage and a count record.

Two separate locks between the medication and unauthorized access, such as a locked box inside a locked cabinet or room. The keys are controlled separately from the general medication key where practicable.
A medication stopped by the prescriber, or one a resident no longer takes because of a changed order, discharge or death.
A medication past its expiration or beyond-use date, or one that is damaged, contaminated or no longer reliably labeled.
A licensed practitioner such as a physician assistant or advanced practice registered nurse who may prescribe or train within the scope of their license.
A documented written and observed demonstration that a staff member can perform medication tasks correctly. It is completed at the end of training and at least every 12 months.

procedures: Locked storage: The Responsible Staff Person (RSP) ensures that all prescription, over-the-counter and emergency medications are kept in a locked cabinet, box or room at every site, in a location staff can reach quickly. Medications are never left unattended during a pass.

Key control: The Administrator assigns keys only to trained, on-duty staff. The on-shift trained staff member holds the keys. The Administrator keeps a key log and re-keys the storage if a key is lost, within 24 hours.

Separation and labeling: Each resident's medications are kept in the original pharmacy-labeled container, separate from other residents' medications. Staff do not repackage, pre-pour, relabel or transfer medications. Only a physician or pharmacist may repackage or dispense.

Order check on receipt: When medication is received, the trained staff member compares the label to the signed order or prescription (signed within the past year) and the MAR before the medication is placed in storage. Any discrepancy goes to the pharmacy or prescriber the same day and is documented.
Refrigerated medications: Staff keep refrigerated medications in a dedicated, lockable container or locked refrigerator, separate from food. A thermometer is kept in the refrigerator.

Temperature log: Staff read and record the temperature every day on the Refrigerator Temperature Log, with the date, time and initials. The safe range is 36-41F. If a reading is outside the range, staff notify the RSP at once, adjust the unit, and call the pharmacist or nurse to decide whether the medication is still usable. The action taken is written on the log.

Controlled substances: Staff store controlled substances under double lock. At every shift change, two staff count them together and sign the Controlled Substance Count Record. Any discrepancy is reported to the RSP and Administrator immediately and handled as a medication incident under MED-03 and ABE-02.

Weekly storage check: The RSP checks storage weekly. The check covers locks, temperatures, expiration dates, labels and the count record. It is documented on the Medication Storage Checklist and filed with the Administrator.

Removing discontinued or out-of-date medications: Staff remove them from active storage the same day they are identified or the order is stopped. They are placed in a labeled, locked quarantine container, separate from active medications, and the MAR is updated.

Disposal of non-controlled medications: Within 30 days, or sooner if the Administrator directs, two staff (or one staff member and the nurse or pharmacist) remove the quarantined medication and return it to the dispensing pharmacy, use a pharmacy or law enforcement take-back option, or render it unusable and unrecoverable by a method permitted by law. Medications are never flushed or placed in trash intact unless a lawful method requires it.

Disposal of controlled substances: Two staff witness the count and the disposal. Controlled substances are returned to the pharmacy, a take-back program or another lawful method, and both witnesses sign. No controlled substance is held by staff after discontinuation without the Administrator's written approval.

Disposal record: The staff member records the resident's name, medication, strength, quantity, reason for disposal, date, method and the signatures of both witnesses on the Medication Disposal Record. Disposal is never done by one person alone.

Resident belongings: A resident's medications are not disposed of when the resident is discharged or moves. They follow the resident as described in ADS-04, with the order, unless the prescriber discontinues them.

Training before any medication task: No staff member administers or assists with medications until trained by a physician, physician extender, RN or pharmacist. Training covers [AGENCY NAME]'s pathways (MED-01), the eight rights, MAR use, storage, emergency medications (epinephrine, seizure rescue, glucagon and naloxone), error reporting and allergy flagging.

Competency testing: The trainer or the Nurse/RN consultant tests each staff member with a written test and a direct observation of a medication pass before the first independent task. The test is repeated at least every 12 months, and after any significant medication error.

Authorized staff list: The Administrator keeps a current Authorized Medication Staff list with each person's training date, trainer name and credentials, and last competency date. Staff whose annual competency has lapsed are removed from medication duties until retested.

Emergency medications: Staff trained under this policy, including non-licensed staff, may give emergency medications (epinephrine, seizure rescue medication, glucagon, naloxone) according to the resident's order and emergency protocol, then call 911 and notify the RSP.

Independent assessment: At least every two years, [AGENCY NAME] obtains a medication-management assessment by an independent pharmacist or RN at every site where medications are kept. The Administrator reviews findings and records corrections in the QA program (QA-01).

responsibilities.duty: Assigns keys, keeps the Authorized Medication Staff list, arranges training and annual competency testing, arranges the biennial independent assessment, and approves disposal of controlled substances.
Completes weekly storage checks, reviews temperature logs and count records, and removes unauthorized staff from medication duties.
Delivers or oversees training, tests competency, advises on temperature excursions and disposal, and assists with the independent assessment.
Keep medications locked, record temperatures daily, count controlled substances each shift, complete disposal with a witness, and report every discrepancy at once.

documentation: Refrigerator Temperature Log (daily)
Controlled Substance Count Record (every shift change)
Medication Storage Checklist (weekly)
Key Log
Medication Disposal Record with two signatures
Authorized Medication Staff list
Medication training records and annual competency test results in the personnel file
Biennial independent pharmacist or RN assessment and corrective action notes

policies.category: Abuse, neglect, exploitation and incident reporting
policies.title: Abuse, Neglect and Exploitation Prevention and Reporting
policies.applies_to: All employees, contractors, volunteers, the Administrator, the Responsible Staff Person and the governing body of [AGENCY NAME], and all residents and their representatives.
policies.purpose: To protect residents from abuse, neglect, exploitation and abandonment, and to make sure every suspected or known event is reported, investigated and corrected promptly.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not tolerate abuse, neglect, exploitation or abandonment of any resident. Every staff member is a mandatory reporter and must report suspected events immediately. Orientation covering mandatory ABE reporting is completed before any direct contact with residents. Residents may report privately to DBHDD or others, even over a guardian's objection, and no one may retaliate against a resident or staff member who reports. The Administrator or designee reports to DBHDD in the form and electronic system DBHDD specifies and conducts a prompt internal investigation. DBHDD may open a separate investigation, and [AGENCY NAME] will cooperate fully. This policy meets 290-9-37-.07(3)(e), procedures for reporting and investigating abuse, neglect, exploitation, incidents, accidents, injuries and changes in a resident's condition, including death, and 82-13-1-.05(8)(f) (proposed), procedures for reporting abuse, neglect, exploitation, incidents, accidents, injuries and changes in a resident's condition, including death. General incident handling is in ABE-02 and death in ABE-03.

definitions.definition: Any act or omission that causes or may cause physical, sexual, verbal, emotional or psychological harm to a resident, including striking, rough handling, threats, humiliation, isolation or unauthorized restraint or seclusion.
Failure to provide the care, supervision, food, medication, hygiene, safety or medical attention a resident needs, whether or not harm results.
Improper use of a resident's money, property, benefits, labor or identity for the benefit of someone else.
Leaving a resident without adequate care or supervision, or without arranging for it.
The DBHDD Regional Field Office developmental disabilities contact designated to receive notices of deaths and high-visibility incidents.
An event likely to draw media, legislative or public attention, or one DBHDD identifies as such in its provider manual.

procedures: Prevention: The Administrator screens staff under STF-03, trains them under STF-04, ensures staffing under STF-01, reviews the Code of Conduct (COC-01) with each employee annually, and encourages residents to speak up about how they are treated.

Orientation: Before any direct contact with a resident, each new employee, contractor and volunteer completes orientation on resident rights, the definitions above, mandatory ABE reporting, the HCBS Settings Rule and this policy. The date is signed and filed in the personnel record. The topic is refreshed in annual training.

Rights posting: The Administrator posts the DBHDD telephone number and the regional field office number [DBHDD REGIONAL FIELD OFFICE PHONE] where residents can read them, and reviews the right to report privately with each resident and representative at admission and at least annually.

Immediate response: Any staff member who sees, suspects or is told of abuse, neglect, exploitation or abandonment first makes the resident safe, separates the resident from the alleged perpetrator, and gets medical care. Staff call 911 if there is an emergency or a crime.

Staff report: The staff member reports to the Administrator or Responsible Staff Person immediately, by phone, at [PHONE]. If the Administrator is the subject of the report or is unreachable, the staff member reports directly to DBHDD. A staff member may also report directly to DBHDD or law enforcement at any time, and does not need anyone's permission to do so.

Notify representative: The Administrator or designee immediately notifies the resident's guardian or representative and emergency contact, unless that person is the alleged perpetrator. In that case, the Administrator notifies DBHDD and the support coordinator and documents the reason.

Report to DBHDD: The Administrator or designee reports to DBHDD in the form and electronic system DBHDD specifies, within the timeline set in the current DBHDD Provider Manual. The Administrator keeps the current reporting-timeline sheet at [LOCATION] and confirms it each quarter. Reports are not delayed to complete the internal investigation.
Death or high-visibility incident: The Administrator or designee also notifies the RSA-DD within 2 hours of any death or high-visibility incident, in addition to the DBHDD report.

Other required reports: The Administrator also reports to law enforcement and any other agency required by law when a crime or legally reportable event is suspected, and records each report in the file.

Protect during investigation: Pending investigation, the Administrator removes any staff member alleged to have abused, neglected or exploited a resident from direct contact with residents and tells the person not to discuss the matter with the resident or witnesses. Personal safety and continuity of care are arranged for the resident.

Investigator and evidence: Within 24 hours the Administrator assigns an investigator who has no conflict of interest, or requests one from [GOVERNING BODY CONTACT]. The investigator preserves evidence, photographs injuries, collects written statements from all involved before the end of the shift where possible, and interviews the resident with support and in privacy.

DBHDD investigation: If DBHDD opens its own investigation, the Administrator gives DBHDD full access to records, staff and residents and does not interfere with or duplicate witness interviews unless DBHDD agrees.

Completion: The investigator completes a written report with findings, evidence and conclusions. The Administrator decides on corrective actions (such as retraining, discipline under COC-02, termination, plan changes or environment changes) and sends required updates to DBHDD.

Resident follow-up: The Administrator confirms the resident has received medical care and emotional support, tells the resident and representative the outcome as allowed by law, and updates the ISP or safety plan if needed.

No retaliation: Staff must not punish, threaten, discipline, reduce hours of or otherwise act against anyone who makes a good-faith report. Retaliation against a staff member or resident is itself a violation and is subject to discipline and further reporting. Concerns about retaliation go to the Administrator or directly to DBHDD.
Quality review: The Administrator includes every ABE event in the QA incident review (QA-01) and the governing body's quarterly review, looking for patterns by staff, shift, resident and location.

responsibilities.duty: Make the resident safe, report suspected abuse, neglect, exploitation or abandonment immediately, cooperate with investigations, and never retaliate.
Ensures orientation and training, reports to DBHDD and the RSA-DD, assigns the investigator, protects residents during the investigation, and implements corrective action.
Receives reports when the Administrator is unavailable, secures the scene and resident safety, and starts documentation.
Receives reports of events and trends, and investigates complaints about the Administrator.
May report privately at any time to DBHDD or any other person or agency.

documentation: Signed orientation and annual ABE training records
Incident and ABE report form
DBHDD report confirmation and RSA-DD notification record
Notifications to representative or guardian, emergency contact and law enforcement
Investigation file: statements, photographs, report and findings
Corrective action record
Posted DBHDD and regional field office numbers (photo or checklist verification)
QA incident log entry

policies.category: Abuse, neglect, exploitation and incident reporting
policies.title: Reportable Incidents, Accidents, Injuries and Investigations
policies.applies_to: All staff of [AGENCY NAME], including the Administrator, the Responsible Staff Person and the Nurse/RN consultant, for any incident, accident, injury or change in condition involving a resident.
policies.purpose: To make sure every incident, accident and injury gets prompt care, notification, reporting, documentation and review, and that the home learns from them.
policies.policy: When a resident has an incident, accident, injury or change in condition, staff immediately obtain the care the resident needs and notify the emergency contact, representative or guardian. The Administrator or designee reports to DBHDD in the form DBHDD accepts, which may be an online platform, and documents a summary with follow-up and notifications. Every injury to a resident is tracked as a required QA indicator. Incidents are reviewed at least weekly and quarterly for trends. DBHDD may open its own investigation of any reportable incident. This policy meets 290-9-37-.07(3)(e), procedures for reporting and investigating abuse, neglect, exploitation, incidents, accidents, injuries, and changes in a resident's condition, including death, and 82-13-1-.05(8)(f) (proposed), procedures for reporting abuse, neglect, exploitation, incidents, accidents, injuries, and changes in a resident's condition, including death. Abuse, neglect and exploitation are also handled under ABE-01, and death under ABE-03.

definitions.definition: Any event outside the resident's normal routine that affects health, safety, rights or property, including medication errors, elopement or missing person, behavioral crisis, use of restraint, fall, property damage and police contact.
An unplanned event, such as a fall or burn, that causes or could cause injury.
Any physical harm to a resident, whatever its cause or severity, including injuries of unknown origin.
An incident that meets the criteria in the current DBHDD Provider Manual or DBHDD instructions and must be reported to DBHDD in the specified system.
A noticeable change in a resident's physical, mental, behavioral or functional status that needs medical review or a change in care.
The QA measure that counts and analyzes all injuries to residents; see QA-01.

procedures: Immediate care: The first staff member present attends to the resident's safety and health, gives first aid within training, and calls 911 for any emergency. Medical care is never delayed to complete paperwork.

Notify the RSP and Administrator: The staff member calls the Responsible Staff Person immediately. The RSP calls the Administrator at [PHONE] as soon as the resident is safe, and no later than the end of the shift.

Notify the resident's contacts: Staff or the RSP immediately notify the resident's emergency contact and representative or guardian, with what happened, the resident's condition and the care given. Staff also notify the prescribing practitioner or nurse when needed for care decisions.

Incident report: Before the end of the shift, the staff member who saw or found the event completes the Incident Report in factual, objective language, with date, time, place, people involved, witnesses, injuries, care given and notifications. Opinions are labeled as such. The Incident Report is never altered after signing; corrections are made as dated addenda.

Injuries of unknown origin: Staff photograph any injury, record its size and location on a body map, and tell the Administrator at once. An injury of unknown origin is treated as possible abuse or neglect and handled under ABE-01 until ruled out.

Administrator review: The Administrator or designee reviews each Incident Report within one business day, decides whether it is a reportable incident under the current DBHDD criteria, and sets follow-up.

Report to DBHDD: For reportable incidents, the Administrator or designee reports in the form and electronic system DBHDD specifies, within the timeline in the DBHDD Provider Manual. The Administrator keeps the current reportable-incident list and timelines at [LOCATION] and confirms them each quarter. Staff attach the confirmation to the incident file.

Investigation: The Administrator reviews the cause of every reportable incident and every injury. For serious or unexplained events, the Administrator assigns an investigator who was not involved, collects statements, reviews the plan, staffing and environment, and writes the findings. DBHDD may open a separate investigation. The Administrator cooperates and provides all records.

Summary and follow-up: The Administrator documents a summary of each event with the investigation, follow-up actions (for example, retraining, equipment repair, supervision changes, medical appointments, ISP or safety plan changes) and each notification, with dates and who made them.

Resident plan: The RSP or nurse makes sure the resident's follow-up care and any plan changes are carried out and shared with the next shift. The ISP team is told when an event shows the plan needs revision.

Weekly review: The Administrator reviews all incidents, accidents and injuries at least weekly, checks that follow-up is complete, and signs the Weekly Incident Review Log. Open items are carried forward until closed.

Injury indicator: Each injury is entered on the QA Injury Indicator Log with the resident, type, cause, location, shift and preventability. Injuries are counted whether or not the incident is reportable to DBHDD.

Quarterly trends: Each quarter the Administrator analyzes incidents and injuries by type, resident, time, staff, site and cause. The findings, including any restrictive-intervention use reviewed by the Rights Sub-Committee, are distributed as the QA plan requires and used to create corrective actions (see QA-01 and QA-02).
Staff training: The Administrator reviews this policy with staff at orientation and annually, and retrains staff when an incident review shows a gap in practice.

responsibilities.duty: Obtain care, report the event to the RSP immediately, complete the Incident Report before shift end, and notify contacts as directed.
Makes sure care is obtained and contacts notified, informs the Administrator, and carries out follow-up on shift.
Decides reportability, reports to DBHDD, investigates, documents the summary, completes weekly review, and presents quarterly trends.
Reviews injuries and changes in condition, advises on care and prevention, and supports the injury indicator analysis.
Reviews quarterly incident and injury data and requires corrective action.

documentation: Incident Report (original and addenda)
Body map and photographs for injuries
Record of notifications (contact, time, staff)
DBHDD report confirmation in the system DBHDD specifies
Investigation file and written summary with follow-up
Weekly Incident Review Log
QA Injury Indicator Log
Quarterly trend analysis and corrective action plans

policies.category: Abuse, neglect, exploitation and incident reporting
policies.title: Death of a Resident
policies.applies_to: All staff of [AGENCY NAME], including the Administrator, the Responsible Staff Person and the Nurse/RN consultant.
policies.purpose: To make sure that when a resident dies, the resident is treated with dignity, the right people are notified at once, the death is reported as required, and the death is reviewed.
policies.policy: When a resident dies, staff immediately notify next of kin, the physician and the representative or guardian. [AGENCY NAME] observes the death-reporting statutes, reports the death to DBHDD, and notifies the RSA-DD within 2 hours. Refunds and transfer of belongings, funds and burial accounts follow the discharge policies. Every death is included in mortality review. This policy meets 290-9-37-.07(3)(e), procedures for reporting and investigating abuse, neglect, exploitation, incidents, accidents, injuries, and changes in a resident's condition, including death, and 82-13-1-.05(8)(f) (proposed), procedures for reporting abuse, neglect, exploitation, incidents, accidents, injuries, and changes in a resident's condition, including death.

definitions.definition: The Georgia laws that require certain deaths to be reported to the coroner or medical examiner and law enforcement, and that govern pronouncement and release of the body.
The family member or other person identified in the resident's record to be contacted at death.
The DBHDD Regional Field Office developmental disabilities contact designated to receive notices of deaths and high-visibility incidents.
A structured review of a death to find contributing factors, check the care provided and identify prevention steps; see QA-02.

procedures: Emergency response: If a resident is found unresponsive or not breathing, staff immediately call 911, start CPR or BLS unless a valid do-not-resuscitate order is on file, and continue until emergency responders take over. Staff do not delay calling 911.
Notify the RSP and Administrator: The staff member immediately tells the Responsible Staff Person, who calls the Administrator at [PHONE] without delay.

Unexpected death or scene: Staff do not move or clean up the scene beyond what is required for resuscitation. Staff preserve medications, equipment, the MAR and the ISP, and give them to authorities if requested.

Notify law enforcement and coroner: The Administrator or RSP follows the Georgia death-reporting statutes, contacts the coroner or medical examiner and law enforcement when the law requires (including sudden, unexpected, unattended or suspicious deaths), and records the name, time and instructions received.

Immediately notify the resident's contacts: The Administrator or designee immediately notifies the next of kin, the resident's physician, and the representative or guardian, by phone. The person gives the facts known, offers support, and tells the family about arrangements. Contacts and times are documented.
Report to DBHDD: The Administrator or designee reports the death to DBHDD in the form and electronic system DBHDD specifies, within the timeline in the current DBHDD Provider Manual.

RSA-DD notice: The Administrator or designee notifies the RSA-DD within 2 hours of the death, by phone or other method DBHDD directs, at [DBHDD REGIONAL FIELD OFFICE PHONE]. The time of the notice and the person reached are recorded.

Incident report and statements: The staff who found or were with the resident complete an Incident Report and written statements before the end of their shift. The Administrator secures the resident's record, MAR, controlled substance counts and recent logs.

ABE screening: The Administrator reviews the circumstances for any sign of abuse, neglect or exploitation. If any exist, the event is also handled under ABE-01. The Administrator cooperates with any investigation by DBHDD, law enforcement or the coroner.

Care of the resident and respect: Staff treat the resident's body with dignity and follow the resident's and family's known cultural, religious and personal wishes. The body is released to the funeral home or authority only as directed by the physician, coroner or medical examiner and the family or representative.

Belongings, funds and burial accounts: The Administrator inventories the resident's belongings, medications, personal funds and any burial account with a second staff witness, and handles them, the refund of any prepaid charges and notice to the representative under ADS-03 and ADS-04.

Medications: Staff secure the resident's medications and dispose of or transfer them under MED-04 and ADS-04, with the MAR documenting the last dose given. Any controlled substances are counted by two staff.

Support for housemates and staff: The Administrator tells the other residents, in a way each understands and with sensitivity, offers support and counseling, and arranges debriefing and support for staff.

Notify funders and teams: The Administrator notifies the support coordinator, the funding source and any other party required by contract or the resident's record, and updates enrollment and billing status as described in GOV-03.

Mortality review: The Administrator includes the death in the next mortality review under QA-02, with the Nurse/RN consultant, collects the records needed, and records findings and any preventive actions.
Record closure: The Administrator completes the death record, retains the resident's record per REC-01, and files the DBHDD report confirmation.

responsibilities.duty: Call 911, start CPR unless a valid DNR is on file, preserve the scene, call the RSP, and complete the incident report and statement.
Leads on-site response, notifies the Administrator, and secures records, medications and belongings until the Administrator arrives.

Ensures notifications to next of kin, physician and representative or guardian, reports to DBHDD and RSA-DD, follows the death-reporting statutes, and manages refunds, belongings and mortality review.
Reviews the health record and supports mortality review.

documentation: Incident Report and staff statements
Notification log (next of kin, physician, representative or guardian, coroner or medical examiner, law enforcement, with times)
DBHDD report confirmation and RSA-DD notification record
Inventory of belongings, funds and burial account
Medication disposition record
Mortality review file
Resident record retained under REC-01

policies.category: Medical support devices and restrictive interventions
policies.title: Medical Support Devices and Restrictive Interventions
policies.applies_to: All staff of [AGENCY NAME], the Administrator, the Responsible Staff Person, the Nurse/RN consultant, the Rights Sub-Committee, and any clinician or prescriber who orders a device or intervention for a resident.
policies.purpose: To identify the medical support devices and restrictive interventions that [AGENCY NAME] implements or prohibits, and to make sure any device is used only when ordered, individualized, least restrictive and monitored.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] permits only medical support devices that meet the conditions below, and permits restraint only as a last resort under RST-02. [AGENCY NAME] prohibits chemical restraint, seclusion, restraint devices that are not medical support devices, and prone restraint. The Rights Sub-Committee reviews the use of restrictive interventions. This policy meets 82-13-1-.05(8)(g) (proposed), procedures that outline and identify the medical support devices and other restrictive interventions that are implemented or prohibited by the organization and licensure requirements as outlined in Sections .16 and .17 of these Rules. It is written to the proposed Chapter 82-13-1 and will be updated if the final adopted rule differs.

definitions.definition: A device that a physician or physician extender prescribes or recommends, that serves a documented medical or therapeutic purpose, and that is the least restrictive option. It is used to support the resident's health, posture, mobility or safety, not to control behavior or for staff convenience.
Any manual, physical or mechanical method that restricts a person's freedom of movement. A medical support device used as ordered is not a restraint.
Use of a medication to control behavior or restrict freedom of movement that is not a standard treatment for the resident's condition. It is prohibited.
Involuntary confinement of a resident alone in a room or area from which the resident is prevented from leaving. It is prohibited.
Holding a person face-down. It is prohibited, even in a nationally benchmarked crisis-intervention program.
Positive Behavior Support Plan; see RST-02.
The committee of [AGENCY NAME] that reviews restrictive interventions for rights, necessity and safety.

procedures: Prohibited practices: No staff member may use chemical restraint, seclusion, prone restraint or any restraint device that is not a medical support device. This includes locked rooms, ties, straps, wrist or ankle restraints, mechanical restraints and medications used to control behavior. Any use is a reportable incident and a violation of the Code of Conduct (COC-01).

Devices [AGENCY NAME] may implement: Only individually ordered medical support devices on the approved list at [DEVICE LIST LOCATION] may be used. The list may include examples such as wheelchair positioning supports and seat belts, protective helmets, gait belts, bed rails and bed or chair positioning supports. No device is used for a resident without the process below, even if it is on the list.

Qualifying test: Before any device is considered, the nurse or team checks that a physician or extender prescribes or recommends it, that it has a documented medical or therapeutic purpose, and that it is the least restrictive option. Less restrictive alternatives tried or considered are documented.

Physician's written order: Before first use, the Administrator obtains a written order from the physician or extender that states the type of device, rationale, duration, how and when it is released, and monitoring. The order is filed in the resident's record.

Discussion with resident and guardian: Before first use, the nurse or Administrator discusses the device, its purpose and alternatives with the resident and the guardian or representative, in a way the resident can understand, and documents their response. The resident's objection is recorded and sent to the ISP team.

Plan authorization: Before first use, the device is authorized in the resident's ISP and PBSP, or crisis/safety plan, and the plan states when it is used, how long, how it is released and monitored. A device that needs these steps is not used on an emergency or convenience basis.

Staff training: The Administrator or Nurse/RN consultant trains each staff member on the use, fitting, release, risks, cleaning and monitoring of the device before the staff member uses it. Training is documented and added to competency testing.
Inspect before every use: Staff inspect the device before each use for damage, fit, wear and cleanliness. A damaged or unsafe device is removed from use and reported to the RSP the same day.

Monitor and document use: Staff follow the monitoring in the order, check skin, circulation, comfort, breathing and position, release as ordered, and record each use on the Device Use Log with date, times, staff and observations. Any problem goes to the nurse immediately.

Review of need: The nurse and ISP team review each device at least every [REVIEW INTERVAL, NOT LONGER THAN THE ORDER DURATION] and whenever the resident's condition changes, to decide if it is still needed and whether a less restrictive option exists.

Discontinuation: A device is stopped only by physician order, or by the team if it is no longer needed or is harmful, followed by an updated order. Staff stop immediately in an emergency and call the physician. The ISP and PBSP are updated.
Restraint in an emergency: Staff may use physical restraint only as a last resort and only according to RST-02. Prohibited practices above are never used, even in an emergency.

Rights Sub-Committee review: The Rights Sub-Committee reviews every use of a restrictive intervention and device-related concerns at least quarterly, checking that required orders, plans, training and monitoring were present, and recommends corrective action to the Administrator (see QA-01).
Incident reporting: Any use of restraint, any use of a prohibited practice, and any injury connected to a device is reported under ABE-02, and to DBHDD where it meets DBHDD's criteria.
Annual review: The Administrator reviews this policy and the approved device list each year with the Rights Sub-Committee and updates them as needed.

responsibilities.duty: Makes sure the order, discussion, plan authorization and training are in place before first use, and enforces the prohibitions.
Applies the qualifying test, obtains orders, trains staff, reviews monitoring and need, and tracks device use.
Prescribes, recommends, reviews and discontinues devices.
Reviews restrictive interventions and devices for rights, necessity and safety.
Inspect and use devices as trained and ordered, monitor, document, and report problems immediately.

documentation: Physician's written order (type, rationale, duration, release, monitoring) in the record
Record of discussion with resident and guardian
ISP and PBSP or crisis/safety plan authorization
Device Use Log and pre-use inspection records
Staff training and competency records
Rights Sub-Committee minutes
Approved device list and annual policy review record

policies.category: Medical support devices and restrictive interventions
policies.title: Minimizing Restraint and Positive Behavior Support
policies.applies_to: All direct support staff, the Responsible Staff Person, the Administrator, the Positive Behavior Support clinician, and the Rights Sub-Committee at [AGENCY NAME].
policies.purpose: To prevent crises through positive behavior support, to minimize the use of restraint to the greatest extent possible, and to protect residents' safety and rights when restraint is used as a last resort.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] has and enforces effective procedures to minimize to the greatest extent possible the use of restraints. Restraint is a last resort, used only when specified in the resident's ISP, PBSP or crisis/safety plan, and only by staff holding current nationally benchmarked crisis-intervention training. Chemical restraint, seclusion, restraint devices that are not medical support devices, and prone restraint are never permitted. This policy meets 82-13-1-.17(3) (proposed): the Community Living Arrangement shall have and enforce effective procedures to minimize to the greatest extent possible the use of restraints. It is written to the proposed Chapter 82-13-1 and will be updated if the final adopted rule differs.

definitions.definition: Restraint is used only after positive supports, de-escalation and less restrictive alternatives have been tried or are clearly unsafe, and only to prevent imminent danger to the resident or others.
Positive Behavior Support Plan: an individualized plan based on a functional assessment that teaches skills, changes the environment and sets responses to behavior.
A written plan that states a resident's known triggers, warning signs, de-escalation steps and the specific response to a crisis.
A recognized crisis-prevention and intervention program that teaches de-escalation and safe physical intervention and is accepted by DBHDD.
Areas such as the chest, back, neck, joints, wrists and ankles where pressure, restricted circulation or restricted breathing could cause harm during a hold.

procedures: Prevention first: The ISP team and clinician use a functional assessment to write a PBSP for any resident with behavior that may put the resident or others at risk. The PBSP lists positive supports, skill teaching, environmental changes and de-escalation steps that staff use before any physical intervention.

Training before involvement: No staff member takes part in a physical intervention without current nationally benchmarked crisis-intervention training. The Administrator keeps the roster of trained staff, with certification dates, and assigns shifts so that a trained staff member is available. Training is documented in the personnel record and refreshed as the program requires.

Plan authorization: Restraint may be used only if the ISP, PBSP or crisis/safety plan specifies it for that resident, with the circumstances, the type of hold allowed and the steps to try first. If a resident has no such plan and a physical emergency occurs, staff use the least force necessary to protect life and then call 911 and the RSP.

Prohibited methods: Staff never use prone restraint, chemical restraint, seclusion, or any restraint device that is not a medical support device, whether or not the program teaches it. Staff never use restraint as punishment, for convenience, or because of short staffing.
De-escalation: Staff try verbal de-escalation, reduced stimulation, choices, space, redirection and the supports in the plan first, and document the interventions tried.

Applying a hold: If a plan-authorized hold is needed for imminent danger, a trained staff member uses the least restrictive hold, for the shortest time, with a second staff member present where possible, watching breathing, color and responsiveness. Staff never put weight on the chest, back or neck or block the airway.
Release when the danger ends: Staff release the resident as soon as the imminent danger ends, even if the planned time has not passed, and stay with the resident to give support.

Checks every 15 minutes: During any restraint, staff check the resident at least every 15 minutes, including breathing, circulation and pressure sites, and record each check. If staff see any sign of distress or injury, they release the resident and call 911 if needed.
Medical review: After any restraint, the nurse or a trained staff member checks the resident for injury and arranges medical care when needed. Injuries are recorded under ABE-02.

Notify representative or guardian: The Administrator or RSP notifies the resident's representative or guardian by phone within 24 hours of any restraint, and documents the date, time and person reached.

Documentation: Within 24 hours, the staff involved complete a Restraint Report with the resident, date, times, staff, the behavior and danger, the interventions tried before, hold used, length of time, each 15-minute check, pressure-site checks, release time, injuries, and notifications.
DBHDD reporting: The Administrator reports any restraint incident that meets DBHDD's criteria in the form and electronic system DBHDD specifies under ABE-02.

Post-event debrief: The Administrator or clinician meets with the staff and, when appropriate, the resident within [NUMBER, NOT MORE THAN 3] business days to find what led to the event, how it could have been prevented, and whether the plan needs to change. The resident's views are recorded.
Plan revision: After any restraint, the ISP team reviews and revises the PBSP or crisis/safety plan as needed, with the aim of eliminating future use.

Monitoring to minimize: The Administrator tracks every use of restraint by resident, staff, shift, time, trigger and length, and shares it with the Rights Sub-Committee, which reviews restrictive interventions at least quarterly and recommends actions to reduce use (see QA-01 and RST-01).
Rights check: Staff may not use restraint to enforce rules, force compliance with routines, or retaliate. Any concern that restraint was misused is reported under ABE-01.

responsibilities.duty: Use positive supports and de-escalation first, use restraint only as trained and authorized in the plan, check the resident at least every 15 minutes, release when danger ends, and document.
Supports staff during a crisis, makes sure checks and medical review are done, and notifies the Administrator.
Ensures staff training and plans, notifies guardians within 24 hours, reports to DBHDD when criteria are met, and tracks restraint use.
Completes the functional assessment, writes and revises the PBSP and crisis/safety plan, and leads post-event debriefs.
Reviews all use of restraint and recommends actions to minimize it.

documentation: ISP, PBSP and crisis/safety plan authorizing restraint
Crisis-intervention training certificates and roster
Restraint Report with interventions tried and all 15-minute and pressure-site checks
Record of guardian or representative phone notification within 24 hours
Incident Report and DBHDD report confirmation when criteria are met
Post-event debrief notes and plan revisions
Restraint tracking log and Rights Sub-Committee minutes

policies.category: Admissions and discharges, refunds, transfer of records and belongings, and cooperative living
policies.title: Admission Process and Admission Agreement
policies.applies_to: Administrator, Responsible Staff Person, nursing staff, intake staff and all staff who speak with prospective residents or their representatives
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] admits only people it is authorized to serve and can safely support, and that every resident and representative receives and understands a complete written admission agreement before moving in.
policies.policy: This policy meets 290-9-37-.07(3)(f) (How the residence handles admissions) and 82-13-1-.05(8)(h) (How the residence handles admissions and discharges, including: ...) (proposed). The admission requirements below follow 82-13-1-.12 (proposed). Items .05(8)(h)1 through .05(8)(h)4 are covered in ADS-02 (discharge, transfer and immediate transfer), ADS-03 (refunds), ADS-04 (transfer of records, belongings, funds and burial accounts) and ADS-05 (cooperative living). The admission agreement refers to each of them. [AGENCY NAME] admits a person only when (1) the person has been authorized or is reimbursed by DBHDD for the service, (2) the Administrator has reviewed the person's records and interviewed the person, (3) a physical examination and TB screening dated within 12 months before admission are on file, (4) the home has an open bed within its licensed capacity (no more than 4 residents under the proposed rule) and the person's needs do not exceed what the home can support (see SCP-01 and ADM-01), and (5) a written admission agreement has been signed by [AGENCY NAME], the resident and the guardian or representative. We provide no services to a person who is not authorized or reimbursed by DBHDD. Because the proposed rules are not yet adopted, this policy also follows the current codified rule and will be reviewed again when the final rule is effective.

definitions.definition: The written contract signed by [AGENCY NAME], the resident and the guardian or representative that sets out services, charges, notice of changes, refunds, valuables, cooperative-living expectations and the discharge and transfer procedure.
A court-appointed guardian or other person legally authorized to act for the resident (see RGT-04).
The DBHDD referral and authorization that identifies the person and the funded service (state-funded or NOW/COMP waiver).
Help that lets the resident read and understand the agreement, such as reading it aloud, plain-language or large-print versions, an interpreter, or assistive technology (see RGT-05).

procedures: The Administrator accepts referrals only through the DBHDD Regional Field Office or another DBHDD-authorized route. Before any admission discussion, the Administrator confirms that [AGENCY NAME] holds a current CLA license and an executed DBHDD contract for the service.
The Administrator logs each referral on the Referral/Intake Log with the date received, referral source, funding source and decision date.

The Administrator confirms that DBHDD has authorized or will reimburse the service for this person. A person receiving NOW or COMP waiver services is not eligible for state-funded services, so the Administrator verifies the funding stream before admission. If authorization cannot be confirmed in writing, the person is not admitted.

The Administrator requests and reviews the person's records, including the most recent assessments, current ISP or service plan, physician orders, medication list, behavior or risk plans, incident history and guardianship papers.

The Administrator interviews the person, in a private setting, with the guardian or representative present when applicable. The interview covers the person's preferences, health and behavior needs, supervision needs and goals. The Administrator also consults the nurse (HLT-01) when health needs are involved.

The Administrator compares the person's needs with the home's staffing, physical plant, nursing oversight and services (SCP-01, ADM-01, STF-01). If the person needs more care than the home can provide, or the bed would exceed licensed capacity, the Administrator declines the admission in writing, gives the reason and, with the referral source, helps find a more suitable setting.

The Administrator confirms that a physical examination and TB screening, each dated within 12 months before the admission date, are on file. If either is missing or older, admission is delayed until it is obtained. The Administrator does not accept an undated or unsigned document.

The Administrator completes the Admission Decision Checklist (authorization, record review, interview, capacity and needs fit, physical exam date, TB screening date) and signs and dates it before the admission date.
At least 5 business days before the planned admission, the Administrator gives the resident and guardian a draft admission agreement for review, so they can ask questions or consult others.

The admission agreement states, at a minimum: the services provided; all charges, including any room and board or personal-needs arrangements permitted by funding rules; the commitment to give at least 60 days' written notice of any change in services or charges; the refund policy (ADS-03); how valuables and personal property are handled (RGT-03); cooperative-living expectations (ADS-05); and the written discharge and transfer procedure, including 30 days' notice and expedited transfer (ADS-02).

The Administrator offers to read the agreement aloud and, as needed, uses plain-language, large-print or translated formats, an interpreter or other reasonable accommodation. The Administrator checks the resident's understanding in the resident's own words and notes the accommodation provided on the Admission Checklist.

The agreement is signed and dated by the Administrator, the resident and the guardian or representative before or on the day of admission. Where the resident cannot sign, the Administrator documents why and the representative signs.

The Administrator gives a complete copy to the resident and a complete copy to the guardian or representative at signing, and records on the signature page the date and manner of delivery. The original is filed in the resident record (REC-01).

On the day of admission, staff give the resident the rights notice, grievance procedure and the posted DBHDD and regional field office telephone numbers (RGT-01, RGT-02), and the nurse reconciles medications (MED-01).

If [AGENCY NAME] proposes a change to services or charges, the Administrator gives the resident and representative written notice at least 60 days before the change takes effect, and files a signed acknowledgment or amended agreement.

The Administrator informs the DBHDD Regional Field Office of the admission date and any required enrollment or authorization updates, and ensures the person is added to the home's roster for staffing and emergency planning purposes (STF-01, EMG-01).
The Administrator reviews the admission file within 30 days after admission to confirm that all required items are present, and reviews this policy at least annually (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Makes all admission decisions, completes the record review and interview, verifies authorization, physical exam and TB dates, and signs the agreement for [AGENCY NAME].
Advises on health needs and medication needs, and reconciles medications at admission.
Welcomes the resident, confirms the resident knows the home's rules and emergency procedures, and follows the admission orders on the day of admission.
Adopts this policy and reviews admission, refusal and retention data (GOV-01, QA-01).
