DBHDD authorization or referral
Record review notes and interview notes
Admission Decision Checklist
Physical exam and TB screening documents (dated within 12 months before admission)
Signed admission agreement, with documented delivery of copies to the resident and guardian
Documentation of reasonable accommodation
Written notices of change (60 days)
Written refusal notices, if any

policies.category: Admissions and discharges, refunds, transfer of records and belongings, and cooperative living
policies.title: Discharge, Transfer and Immediate Transfer
policies.applies_to: Administrator, Responsible Staff Person, nursing staff and all staff involved in a resident's move
policies.purpose: To make sure a resident is discharged or transferred only for permitted reasons, with proper notice, safe planning and a full handoff to the receiving provider.
policies.policy: This policy meets 290-9-37-.07(3)(g) (Procedures for discharge and immediate transfers), 82-13-1-.05(8)(h)1 (Procedures for discharge/transfer/immediate transfer due to medical or behavioral needs of residents) (proposed) and 82-13-1-.13(1) (proposed), which requires each admission agreement to include a written procedure for handling discharge and transfer that complies with these rules. The procedure below is attached to, and summarized in, every admission agreement (ADS-01). [AGENCY NAME] gives the resident and representative 30 days' written notice with the reason, and sends a copy to the DBHDD regional field office. An expedited (immediate) transfer is permitted only when (a) the resident needs continuous medical or nursing care beyond what the CLA can provide, or (b) the resident's behavior directly and substantially threatens the health or safety of the resident or others. Within 24 hours of any discharge or transfer, [AGENCY NAME] provides a full file to the receiving provider and documents the reason, notifications and destination. [AGENCY NAME] does not discharge a resident to an unsafe or unknown place, and does not discharge or threaten discharge as retaliation for a complaint (RGT-02).

definitions.definition: The end of a resident's stay with [AGENCY NAME] because of the resident's choice, a change in funding, a move to a waiver, a change in need or a policy-based reason.
A move from this home to another residence, provider or level of care.

A transfer on less than 30 days' notice because continuous medical or nursing care beyond the CLA's capability is needed, or because the resident's behavior directly and substantially threatens health or safety.
The next residence, hospital, nursing facility, family or other provider that will serve the resident.
The regional DBHDD office for the home's region, [PHONE], to which notices are copied.

procedures: Permitted reasons for discharge or transfer are: the resident or representative asks to move; the resident's needs exceed what the home can safely provide (ADM-01); non-payment or loss of DBHDD authorization or funding, including DBHDD disenrollment from state-funded services when the resident moves to a NOW or COMP waiver, on at least 30 days' written notice; the resident's behavior directly and substantially threatens health or safety; or closure of the home or loss of license (with notice under GOV-02).

Before any discharge or transfer notice is issued, the Administrator meets with the resident, the representative, the ISP team and the nurse, and documents the efforts made to meet the resident's needs through additional supports, a revised ISP or behavior support (PCS-01, RST-02).

For a planned discharge or transfer, the Administrator gives the resident and the representative written notice at least 30 days before the move. The notice states the reason, the proposed date, the right to discuss and complain about the decision to DBHDD, the regional field office telephone number and the grievance procedure (RGT-02).
On the same day the notice is issued, the Administrator sends a copy to the DBHDD regional field office and notes the date and method of delivery on the Discharge/Transfer Log.

The Administrator, with the ISP team and the referral source, identifies a suitable destination, arranges a visit if possible, and confirms the receiving provider can meet the resident's needs. Discharge to the street, a shelter or an unidentified location is not permitted.

The Administrator uses an expedited transfer only if, after consultation with the nurse or the resident's physician (for medical needs) or the ISP team or behavior clinician (for behavior), the facts show continuous medical or nursing care beyond the CLA's capability or behavior that directly and substantially threatens health or safety. The Administrator records the specific facts and the persons consulted before the transfer when possible, and no later than 24 hours after.
If there is immediate danger, staff call 911 first, use the emergency steps in HLT-03 and ABE-02, and then follow the steps below. Staff do not use restraint or seclusion except as RST-01 allows.

For an expedited transfer, the Administrator tells the resident, the representative, the DBHDD regional field office and the referral source of the reason, destination and date as soon as the decision is made and no later than the same day, and gives written notice with the reason within 24 hours.

The Administrator gives the resident a written statement of the right to complain to DBHDD and the right to report abuse, neglect or exploitation privately, and tells the resident how to reach the DBHDD and the regional field office (RGT-01, RGT-02).

Within 24 hours of the discharge or transfer, the Administrator or designee provides the receiving provider with a full file, digital or paper, as detailed in ADS-04, and records the date, time, method and the name of the receiving person.

On the day of transfer, staff complete the signed inventory and handoff of medications, belongings, funds and supplies (ADS-04) and give a nurse-to-nurse or nurse-to-provider verbal handoff on current health needs, risks, diet, medication, allergies and behavior supports.

The Administrator completes the Discharge/Transfer Record, which states the reason, the dates of all notices, who was notified (resident, representative, DBHDD regional field office, referral source, physician), the destination with address and contact, and the date the full file was delivered.

If the resident is hospitalized and the home cannot safely accept the resident back, the Administrator follows this policy, including the 30-day or expedited rules, and does not bar the resident's return without documenting the reason.
The Administrator calculates and issues any refund under ADS-03 and reports incidents or deaths as required by ABE-02, ABE-03 and REC-02.
A discharge or transfer for non-compliance with home policy follows RAC-01 first. The notice and the 30-day or expedited criteria are not waived.
The Administrator reports every discharge or transfer, including the reason, to the Governing Body and reviews it in the quarterly QA indicator review (QA-01).

responsibilities.duty: Decides on discharge or transfer, issues notices, copies the DBHDD regional field office, completes the record and ensures the full file is delivered within 24 hours.
Gives clinical input on capability limits, prepares the health summary and medication handoff.
Carries out the inventory and handoff on shift and keeps the resident safe and calm during the move.
Helps find alternatives and a suitable destination.

documentation: Written 30-day notice with reason and proof of delivery
Copy to DBHDD regional field office with date and method
Expedited transfer justification, with names of persons consulted
Discharge/Transfer Record (reason, notifications, destination)
Record of full file delivery within 24 hours
Signed inventory and handoff
Discharge/Transfer Log

policies.category: Admissions and discharges, refunds, transfer of records and belongings, and cooperative living
policies.title: Refunds on Transfer, Discharge or Death
policies.applies_to: Administrator, billing/finance staff and the Responsible Staff Person
policies.purpose: To ensure that any money owed to a resident, or to the resident's estate, is calculated fairly, documented in writing and returned promptly when the resident is transferred, discharged or dies.
policies.policy: This policy meets 290-9-37-.07(3)(h) (How refunds are handled when a resident is transferred, is discharged, or dies) and 82-13-1-.05(8)(h)2 (How refunds are handled when a resident is transferred, is discharged, or dies) (proposed). The refund policy is stated in each admission agreement (ADS-01). The rule text reviewed does not set a refund deadline, so [AGENCY NAME] sets its own: any refund owed is paid within 15 calendar days after the effective date of the transfer, discharge or death, and resident personal funds are returned at the time of departure (or within 3 business days after a death) as described below. Refunds are calculated in writing and paid to the resident, the representative or the estate. Resident funds are always kept and accounted for separately from [AGENCY NAME] operating funds (RGT-03). A refund policy may not require a resident to give up a right, and a resident may not be charged for days after the departure date except as stated in the admission agreement.

definitions.definition: Any prepaid charge, deposit or other amount that [AGENCY NAME] holds and that exceeds the amount earned through the effective date, to be returned to the resident, representative or estate.
The date the resident leaves or dies, or, if later, the date through which the admission agreement says charges continue.
Money belonging to the resident, including personal needs allowance, that [AGENCY NAME] may hold on the resident's request (RGT-03). It is never a [AGENCY NAME] asset.
The executor, administrator or other person with legal authority to receive the deceased resident's money.

procedures: The admission agreement states the refund policy in plain language, including how prepaid charges and any deposit are prorated and the 15-calendar-day refund deadline set by [AGENCY NAME]. The Administrator explains it to the resident and representative at admission.
When a transfer, discharge or death occurs, the Administrator notifies the billing/finance staff the same day and states the effective date.

Within 5 business days after the effective date, finance staff prepare a written Refund Calculation. It shows (a) the amount paid by or for the resident, (b) the daily rate and number of days earned, (c) any deposit held, (d) any amount owed to [AGENCY NAME] that the agreement allows, with the basis, and (e) the net refund. The Administrator reviews and signs it.

Charges are prorated by the day through the effective date only. No charge is made for a notice period when [AGENCY NAME] initiated the discharge, or when the transfer was an expedited transfer by [AGENCY NAME] (ADS-02).

Funds the resident entrusted to [AGENCY NAME] (personal funds, personal needs allowance) are not part of the refund calculation and are not offset against any amount owed. They are returned in full as described in steps 6 and 7 and ADS-04.
For a transfer or discharge, personal funds are reconciled against the resident ledger (RGT-03) and handed to the resident or representative, with signed receipt, on the day of departure.

For a death, personal funds and any refund are reconciled the same day, held in a secure account separate from operating funds and paid only to the legally authorized estate representative or as state law directs, after proof of authority is collected. The Administrator documents the date and name of anyone who receives funds.

A refund check or electronic payment is issued within 15 calendar days of the effective date. It is payable to the resident, the representative or the estate, never to a staff member. The refund and the Refund Calculation are sent to the recipient with a letter explaining how the refund was calculated.

If a refund cannot be delivered because the recipient cannot be found, the Administrator documents at least 3 attempts (phone, mail, regional field office), holds the money separately and follows state requirements for unclaimed property, and records each step.

If [AGENCY NAME] received Medicaid or DBHDD payment for days after the resident left or died, the Administrator corrects the claim and returns the overpayment in accordance with GOV-03, and does not retain it as a resident refund or as revenue.
The resident or representative who disagrees with a Refund Calculation may file a grievance (RGT-02). The Administrator reviews it within 10 business days and corrects any error.
Finance staff file the Refund Calculation, proof of payment and receipt in the resident record (REC-01), and the Administrator reports refund timeliness at the quarterly QA review (QA-01).
The Administrator checks refund timeliness during the annual policy review (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Approves the refund calculation, ensures payment within 15 calendar days, and verifies the legal authority of the recipient.
Prepare the written calculation, reconcile resident funds and issue payment from the correct account.
Notifies the Administrator of any departure or death on the same shift.
Reviews refund timeliness and complaints about refunds.

Written Refund Calculation signed by the Administrator
Proof of payment (check copy or electronic confirmation)
Signed receipt or proof of delivery
Resident fund ledger reconciliation
Proof of authority of the estate representative
Records of attempts to deliver undeliverable refunds
Claim correction records, if any

policies.title: Transfer of Records, Medications, Belongings, Funds and Burial Accounts
policies.applies_to: Administrator, nursing staff, Responsible Staff Person and all staff who prepare or hand off a resident's file, medications or belongings
policies.purpose: To ensure that, when a resident moves, the resident's complete record, unused special medical supplies, belongings, medications, funds and burial accounts go with the resident, are inventoried, and are received and signed for.
policies.policy: This policy meets 82-13-1-.05(8)(h)3 (How the resident's complete record, unused special medical supplies, personal belongings, medications, funds and burial accounts are transferred when a resident is transferred or discharged) (proposed). Within 24 hours of discharge or transfer, [AGENCY NAME] provides the complete file, digital or paper, to the receiving provider (82-13-1-.13, proposed). Disclosure of the record to the receiving provider for treatment and care coordination is permitted under 45 CFR 164.506, and the Administrator limits the disclosure to what the receiving provider needs for continuity of care, subject to CONF-01 and any heightened protections for substance use or other specially protected information. Every item is released only against a signed inventory and handoff form. The reason for the move, who was notified and the destination are documented.

definitions.definition: The resident's record as described in REC-01: face sheet, admission agreement, ISP, assessments, physician orders, medication administration records, health and behavior plans, incident summaries, consents, guardianship papers and funds ledger. Business and personnel records of [AGENCY NAME] are not included.
Unused items prescribed or purchased for the resident, such as wound-care supplies, incontinence supplies, nutrition supplies, adaptive devices and equipment.
A pre-need burial contract, insurance policy or account set aside for the resident's burial that [AGENCY NAME] knows of or manages.
The form on which each item, including its count or amount, is listed and signed by the staff member releasing it and the person receiving it.

procedures: When a discharge or transfer date is set, the Administrator assigns a staff member and the nurse to prepare the transfer package and records the assignments, with a target 'package ready' date at least 2 days before the move for a planned transfer.

The Administrator or designee assembles the complete file (digital or paper) and checks it against the file contents list in REC-01. The nurse prepares a one-page transition summary: diagnoses, allergies, current medications, diet and texture, seizure and choking risks, behavior supports, equipment, appointments and contacts.

Before releasing the file, the Administrator confirms the identity and role of the receiving provider and logs the disclosure as a treatment disclosure under 45 CFR 164.506. If the file includes specially protected information, the Administrator obtains the required consent before disclosure.

Within 24 hours of the discharge or transfer, the Administrator or designee gives the complete file to the receiving provider by secure electronic transfer or by hand or secure courier. The record shows date, time, method and the name of the receiver. Unsecured e-mail and unencrypted media are not used (CONF-01). If a hospital or emergency transfer occurs after hours, the file or a copy goes on the next business day and no later than the 24-hour limit.

Medications: the nurse and a second staff member count each medication, including controlled substances, against the medication administration record. Prescription medications that belong to the resident and are current go with the resident, in the original labeled containers, with the last dose given recorded. Discontinued, expired or unlabeled medications are not released and are disposed of under MED-04.
The nurse tells the receiving provider by phone about the last dose times, any recent medication changes, allergies and missed doses and records the name of the person who took the report.

Special medical supplies and equipment: staff list all unused supplies and resident-owned equipment, pack them and send them with the resident. Supplies bought with the resident's funds go with the resident.

Personal belongings: with the resident (and representative where possible), two staff members list every item on the inventory, starting from the admission inventory and the property list (RGT-03), and note anything missing or damaged. The resident or representative checks the list. Items are packed and released only to the resident or representative or the receiving provider with a signature.

Funds: staff reconcile the resident's ledger and count cash with a second staff member. All money is returned in full, with a signed receipt, and any bank or benefit account information is given to the representative. Staff notify Social Security or other benefit payers as required by RGT-03 and the representative payee rules.

Burial accounts: the Administrator identifies any pre-need contract, insurance policy or account, gives copies to the resident or representative and the receiving provider, and returns control of the account to the resident or the representative in writing. [AGENCY NAME] does not hold, spend or retain a resident's burial funds.

The person receiving the resident, medications, belongings, funds and file signs the Inventory and Handoff form. The Administrator signs it, and a copy is given to the receiver and one is filed in the resident record. Any item that cannot be released is listed with the reason and a plan for delivery within 5 business days.

If the resident dies, the same steps are used as far as they apply. The file is retained by [AGENCY NAME] under REC-01, and belongings, funds and burial information are released only to the legally authorized representative or as directed by law (ABE-03, ADS-03).

The Administrator documents the reason for the move, who was notified (resident, representative, DBHDD regional field office, physician, referral source) and the destination in the Discharge/Transfer Record (ADS-02).

[AGENCY NAME] keeps a copy or the original of the record in accordance with REC-01 after the file is transferred. If the receiving provider reports missing items, the Administrator investigates and sends corrected items within 2 business days.
The Administrator audits all transfer packets quarterly for completeness and timeliness and reports the results to QA (QA-01).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures that the complete file reaches the receiving provider within 24 hours, signs the inventory and documents the reason, notifications and destination.
Prepares the transition summary, counts and releases medications, and gives the verbal handoff.
Inventories belongings, counts funds with a second staff member and obtains signatures.
Checks and signs for the items received.

documentation: Transfer package checklist
Transition summary
Disclosure log (45 CFR 164.506)
Record of file delivery within 24 hours (date, time, method, receiver)
Medication count and release record
Belongings inventory, funds receipt and burial account notice
Signed Inventory and Handoff form
Discharge/Transfer Record

policies.title: Cooperative Living Expectations
policies.applies_to: Administrator, Responsible Staff Person, all direct care staff, residents and representatives
policies.purpose: To set out, in the admission agreement and in daily practice, reasonable expectations for living together in a shared home, without limiting any resident right.
policies.policy: This policy meets 290-9-37-.07(3)(i) (Expectations regarding cooperative living) and 82-13-1-.05(8)(h)4 (Expectations regarding cooperative living) (proposed). Cooperative-living expectations are stated in the admission agreement (82-13-1-.12, proposed) and are explained to every resident and representative before admission. They are courtesy and safety expectations that all residents share, and they may not override resident rights under 82-13-1-.15 (proposed), including bedroom privacy, private communication, visitors at agreed times, telephone access, control of personal property and management of own money (RGT-01). Residents are not staff and may not be required to do staff tasks or chores. A resident may take part in household tasks only when the ISP documents the resident's voluntary choice to do so (PCS-01). No more than 2 residents share a bedroom. [AGENCY NAME] does not punish a resident, restrict food, money, visits or community access, or threaten discharge because of a cooperative-living issue (RAC-01).

definitions.definition: Shared living in which residents and staff respect each other's space, safety, health and belongings in a common home.
A resident's informed and uncoerced choice, recorded in the ISP, to take part in a household task, with no penalty for declining or stopping.
Work that [AGENCY NAME] must provide, such as cleaning common areas, cooking meals for the household, laundry for others, supervision, transport or personal care for another resident.

procedures: The Administrator writes the cooperative-living section of the admission agreement in plain language. It lists expectations such as treating others with respect, not harming people or property, sharing common spaces fairly, keeping noise to reasonable levels at night, cleaning up after oneself, following safety rules on smoking, alcohol and weapons, and giving notice of absences.

Before the agreement is signed, the Administrator reads or explains the section to the resident and representative with accommodations as needed (RGT-05), and records on the Admission Checklist that this was done (ADS-01).

The Administrator checks every proposed expectation against resident rights. Any expectation that would restrict privacy, visitors, telephone use, personal property, money, communication or religious or community activity is removed from the agreement. The agreement states that these rights are not limited by cooperative-living expectations.

The Administrator assigns bedrooms with no more than 2 residents per bedroom. Residents are asked about roommate preference, and a resident may request a room change, which is answered within 10 business days. Staff knock and wait for permission before entering a bedroom except in an emergency (RGT-01).

Staff do not require any resident to clean, cook for, supervise, bathe, dress or transport another resident, or to do any other work that belongs to staff. Household work is staff work unless the resident chooses to take part.

If a resident wishes to help with household tasks, the ISP team documents in the ISP the task, the days and times, the resident's choice, that the resident may stop at any time without penalty, and any payment due under law. Staff review the choice every ISP review and whenever the resident says they no longer want to take part.

The home holds a house meeting at least monthly, where residents may raise issues, choose menus and activities, and suggest changes. Staff keep a brief record of topics raised and follow-up action. Attendance is optional.

When a conflict arises between residents, staff first listen to each person privately, help find a solution with the people involved, and offer a change in seating, bedroom, schedule or activities. They record the conflict and the steps taken in the daily notes (PCS-01).

If an incident involves threats, harm, theft or damage, staff follow ABE-01 and ABE-02 and report it. They do not treat resident-on-resident harm as a cooperative-living issue to be handled informally.

When a resident's behavior repeatedly conflicts with expectations, the Administrator meets with the resident, the representative and the ISP team to find the cause, which may be unmet need, health, roommate or communication, and adds supports (RST-02, RAC-01). Discharge for conduct may happen only as ADS-02 allows.
Staff tell residents that they may complain to the Administrator, to DBHDD or to the regional field office about any cooperative-living rule, and may do so without retaliation (RGT-02).

The Administrator reviews each year, with the residents, the cooperative-living section for fairness and consistency with rights, and records changes. Changes to the agreement require 60 days' written notice (ADS-01).
Rights violations related to cooperative living, including forced chores or privacy intrusions, are tracked as a rights-violation indicator in the QA program (QA-01).

responsibilities.duty: Writes and reviews the expectations, checks them against rights, assigns bedrooms (no more than 2 per room) and handles complaints.

responsibilities.role: Responsible Staff Person and direct care staff
responsibilities.duty: Apply the expectations respectfully, never require resident labor and report conflicts and rights concerns.
Documents any voluntary participation in household tasks and reviews it regularly.
Are asked to follow the shared expectations and are encouraged to raise concerns.

documentation: Cooperative-living section of the signed admission agreement
Admission Checklist entry showing the section was explained
Bedroom assignment and roommate request records
ISP entries for any voluntary household participation
House meeting records
Conflict notes and follow-up
Rights-violation tracking log

policies.title: Internal Quality Assurance Program and Injury Indicator
policies.applies_to: Governing Body, Administrator, Responsible Staff Person, nursing staff and all staff who record or report data
policies.purpose: To measure how well [AGENCY NAME] is protecting and serving residents, find problems early, and correct them, with resident injury as a required measured indicator.
policies.policy: This policy meets 290-9-37-.07(3)(j) (The quality assurance procedures that shall be used to maintain or improve the quality of care and services provided to the residents, including indicators of performance that shall be routinely measured and evaluated; at a minimum, any injury to a resident is an indicator to be measured and improved) and 82-13-1-.05(8)(i) (The internal quality assurance procedures that shall be used to minimize risk and maintain or improve the quality of care and services, including processes for how deficiencies and risks are identified and managed on an ongoing basis; at a minimum, any injury to a resident is an indicator) (proposed). [AGENCY NAME] keeps a written Quality Improvement (QI) plan that is reviewed at least annually, following the DBHDD Developmental Disabilities Provider Manual, Part II, Section 1, Organizational Practices, C. The plan monitors incidents, complaints, rights violations, restrictive interventions, medication management, infection control, confidentiality breaches, ISP implementation and community integration. Indicators are reviewed quarterly and findings are shared. Each quarter at least 4 records, or 5% of individuals served, whichever is greater, are reviewed and the review results are kept for 2 years. Resident injury is always an indicator that is measured, analyzed and improved.

definitions.definition: A measure that is collected the same way each period, so that the home can compare results, spot trends and set targets.

The count and rate of resident injuries, from any cause, including falls, wounds, burns, bruises, fractures, restraint-related injuries and resident-to-resident injuries, along with severity, location, time, cause and action taken.
A quarterly check of resident records against a standard tool to find missing documentation, plan or rule violations and care gaps.
The group within [AGENCY NAME] that reviews every use of a restrictive intervention (RST-01) and rights concerns.
The written plan describing indicators, data sources, responsible persons, schedule, targets and how findings lead to action.

procedures: The Governing Body adopts a written QI plan before opening and appoints the Administrator (or a named QI lead) to run it (GOV-01). The plan lists each indicator, how it is measured, who collects it, how often, the target and who acts on it.

The plan includes at least these risk areas: (a) incidents, (b) complaints and grievances, (c) rights violations, (d) restrictive interventions, (e) medication management, including errors and omissions, (f) infection control, (g) confidentiality breaches, (h) ISP implementation, and (i) community integration. It also includes resident injury as the required indicator.

Injury indicator: staff report every resident injury, however minor, on the Incident/Injury Report on the same shift (ABE-02). The Administrator enters it in the Injury Log with the date, time, resident, type, body part, severity (first aid only, outside medical care, emergency room, hospital stay), place, cause, staff present, supervision level and action taken.

Each month the Administrator totals injuries and calculates the rate per 1,000 resident days. At least quarterly, the QI lead looks for patterns by resident, type, time of day, location, shift, staff, activity and supervision level and compares each quarter to prior quarters.

For any injury of unknown cause, repeated injuries to the same resident, injuries requiring emergency or hospital care, or injuries linked to a restraint or a resident-to-resident event, the Administrator and nurse complete a root-cause review within 7 days. They decide whether to change the ISP, supervision, environment, equipment, training or staffing, and record the decision (ABE-02, OBS-01).

The QI lead sets a target for each indicator, such as no injuries of unknown cause left unexplained and a downward trend in injury rate, and when a target is missed writes a corrective action with the responsible person and the due date.

Medication indicators: the nurse totals medication errors, omissions and refusals each month and reports the types and causes (MED-03). Infection indicators track outbreaks, illnesses and infestations (INF-01). Confidentiality indicators track breaches (CONF-01).

Restrictive interventions are reviewed by [AGENCY NAME]'s Rights Sub-Committee each time they occur, and the Sub-Committee reports use, duration and outcomes quarterly. The Sub-Committee looks for use that is unwarranted, repeated or against RST-01 and recommends positive supports (RST-02).

Each quarter, the QI lead reviews at least 4 resident records or 5% of individuals served, whichever is greater. If fewer than 4 individuals are served, all records are reviewed. The review uses the standard Record Review Tool and checks the ISP, daily documentation, health follow-up, medication records, consents, incident follow-up and community integration (PCS-01, PCS-02, REC-01).

Within 14 days of the end of each quarter, the QI lead prepares a written Quarterly QI Report showing each indicator, the injury rate and trend, record review results, corrective actions and their status.

The QI lead distributes the report to the Governing Body, the Administrator, the nurse, the Responsible Staff Person and direct care staff, and presents it to residents and representatives in an understandable form on request. The advisory board reviews it at least semi-annually (QA-02). Findings are discussed at the next staff meeting.

Corrective actions are tracked until closed and verified by follow-up measurement. A corrective action is closed only when the follow-up data show the problem is fixed or the Governing Body accepts the explanation in writing.

Quality findings are reported to the Governing Body at least quarterly, and any pattern of abuse, neglect, exploitation, serious injury or death is reported to the Governing Body immediately (ABE-01, ABE-03). Required external reports are made under REC-02 and QA-02.

The QI plan is reviewed and updated at least annually, taking into account the prior year's results, survey findings (GOV-02), resident and family input and changes in rules, and the Governing Body signs the new plan.
[AGENCY NAME] keeps quarterly record reviews, QI reports and corrective action records for at least 2 years, and the records are available to DBHDD surveyors on request.

responsibilities.duty: Adopts the QI plan, reviews quarterly reports, sets priorities and approves resources for corrective action.
Maintains the Injury Log and indicators, conducts the quarterly record review, writes the reports and tracks corrective actions.
Provides health, injury, medication and infection data and takes part in root-cause reviews.
Reviews each use of restrictive interventions and rights concerns.
Report injuries and incidents promptly and accurately and carry out corrective actions.

documentation: Written QI plan with annual review date and Governing Body signature
Injury Log and monthly injury rate calculations
Root-cause reviews for serious or unexplained injuries
Quarterly QI Reports with distribution list
Record Review Tool results (at least 4 records or 5% of individuals each quarter, kept 2 years)
Rights Sub-Committee minutes
Corrective action tracking log
Records of reports to the Governing Body and advisory board

policies.title: Quality Reporting, Mortality Review and Advisory Oversight
policies.applies_to: Governing Body, Administrator, QA/QI Coordinator, Rights Sub-Committee, Advisory Board, nursing and clinical staff, and all staff who report incidents or data
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] reports quality data on schedule, reviews every resident death, keeps independent advisory oversight, and uses what it learns to lower risk. This policy works with QA-01 and sets out the reporting, mortality review and oversight parts of the quality assurance program.
policies.policy: This policy meets 82-13-1-.05(8)(i) (proposed): the internal quality assurance procedures used to minimize risk and maintain or improve quality of care, including how deficiencies and risks are identified and managed on an ongoing basis, with injury to a resident as a required indicator. [AGENCY NAME] keeps a written Quality Improvement (QI) plan and reviews it at least annually. The plan monitors incidents, complaints, rights violations, restrictive interventions, medication management, infection control, confidentiality breaches, ISP implementation and community integration. Injury to a resident is a standing indicator that is measured every quarter and acted on when results are worse than expected. Indicator data are reviewed quarterly and the findings are shared with the Governing Body, staff and the Advisory Board. Quality Management (QM) reports are submitted on the DBHDD schedule: October 16, January 17, April 17 and July 17 (FY27). Every resident death is reviewed through a mortality review, and the results feed the QI plan. [AGENCY NAME] earns and keeps an ASO Quality Review score of 85% or higher and follows DBHDD Policy 02-703. An Advisory Board meets at least semi-annually. The Governing Body receives a quarterly report on any contracted providers. The proposed Chapter 82-13-1 is still in rulemaking. [AGENCY NAME] follows the current codified rules and the DBHDD Provider Manual, and the Administrator will update this policy when the final rules take effect (see GOV-04).

definitions.definition: The written annual plan that lists the risk areas monitored, the indicators measured, who reviews them, how often, and what action follows.
A measure of resident injuries, such as injuries per 1,000 resident days broken down by type, severity, location, time of day and cause, used to find patterns and reduce harm.
A structured, documented review of a resident's death to look for care, system or environmental factors that could be improved.
The internal committee that reviews every use of a restrictive intervention and other rights restrictions.
DBHDD's quality review of providers through its Administrative Services Organization. [AGENCY NAME] must keep a score of 85% or higher.

procedures: The Administrator names a QA/QI Coordinator in writing and records the name in the QI plan. The Coordinator owns the quarterly calendar, data collection and report submission.
The Governing Body approves the written QI plan and reviews it at least once each year. The review and any changes are recorded in the Governing Body minutes.

By the 5th day of each month, the Coordinator collects data for the prior month from incident reports (ABE-02), grievances (RGT-02), restrictive intervention records (RST-01), medication error reports (MED-03), infection logs (INF-01), confidentiality breach reports (CONF-01), ISP implementation and community integration records (PCS-01, PCS-02).

The Coordinator updates the injury indicator each month. It records the number of resident injuries, injuries per 1,000 resident days, type, severity, location, cause, whether the injury was preventable, and the follow-up taken.

Each quarter, the QI committee meets to review all indicators. The committee is the Administrator, the Coordinator, the nurse, the Responsible Staff Person and at least one direct-care staff member. It compares results with the prior quarter and with the targets in the QI plan.

When an indicator is worse than target, or the injury indicator shows a pattern, the committee writes a corrective action. The action names the person responsible and a due date, and the committee checks it at the next quarterly meeting. This is how deficiencies and risks are identified and managed on an ongoing basis.

Each quarter, the Coordinator reviews at least 4 resident records or 5% of residents, whichever is greater. The review checks ISP implementation, documentation, health follow-up and rights. Findings and any corrections are written down and kept for 2 years.

The Coordinator prepares the Quarterly QM Report and submits it through the DBHDD/ASO channel by the due dates: October 16, January 17, April 17 and July 17 (FY27). The Administrator signs off before submission. If a due date falls on a weekend or holiday, the report goes in the prior business day.

The Rights Sub-Committee reviews every use of a restrictive intervention and every other rights restriction at least quarterly. It records whether each use met policy (RST-01, RST-02) and what changes it recommended. Its report goes into the QI review.

Within 5 business days of a resident's death, the Administrator reports it as required by ABE-03 and opens a mortality review. The review is done by the nurse, the Administrator and a clinician or physician reviewer (or the resident's physician where available) and finishes within 30 days of the death or sooner if the autopsy or records are delayed.

The mortality review looks at the resident's health history, recent changes of condition, response to symptoms, medication and treatment records, emergency response, incident history, and whether the death was expected. It ends with written findings and any system changes needed.

The Coordinator enters mortality review findings and every reportable incident into the QI data set. Trends from these sources are presented to the QI committee and used to adjust staffing, training, health monitoring or the environment.

The Administrator tracks the ASO Quality Review score. If a review result is below 85%, or a deficiency is cited, the Administrator writes a corrective action plan within the time DBHDD allows and reports it to the Governing Body (see GOV-02).

The Advisory Board meets at least every six months. The Administrator gives it the QI indicator results, injury indicator trends, mortality review summaries (without identifying information) and corrective action status. Minutes record attendance and the Board's recommendations.

If [AGENCY NAME] contracts with another provider (CRA subcontracting is limited to Host Home Providers), the Administrator reports on those contracted providers to the Governing Body every quarter. The report also goes to the Regional Field Office before the end of FY Q1 and Q3.

The Coordinator shares QI findings every quarter with staff at a team meeting and posts a summary for residents and representatives in plain language. Corrective actions and changes are described in the next quarter's report.
The Coordinator keeps all QI plans, data, committee minutes, reports and corrective actions in the QA file. Quality review records are kept at least 2 years (see REC-01).

responsibilities.duty: Approves and annually reviews the QI plan, reviews quarterly findings and contracted provider reports, and ensures corrective actions are completed.
Signs QM reports before submission, tracks the ASO Quality Review score, leads mortality reviews and ensures staff take part in QI.
Collects and analyzes data, keeps the injury indicator, schedules committee meetings, prepares and submits quarterly reports and keeps the QA file.
Joins mortality reviews and the QI committee and advises on health-related indicators and injury prevention.
Reviews every restrictive intervention and rights restriction and reports its findings into the QI review.
Meets at least semi-annually, reviews quality data and makes recommendations to the Governing Body.
Report incidents, injuries and concerns accurately and on time so the indicators are reliable.

documentation: Written QI plan with Governing Body annual review minutes
Monthly indicator data and the injury indicator worksheet
Quarterly QI committee minutes and corrective action log
Quarterly record review results (kept 2 years)
Submitted Quarterly QM Reports with dates of submission
Rights Sub-Committee minutes and reports
Mortality review reports and findings
ASO Quality Review results and any corrective action plan
Advisory Board minutes and attendance
Quarterly contracted-provider reports to the Governing Body and reports to the Regional Field Office

policies.category: Staffing, staff training and credential verification
policies.title: Staffing Requirements, Coverage Plans and Awake Staff
policies.applies_to: Administrator, Responsible Staff Person, scheduling staff, and all direct-care staff
policies.purpose: To make sure that each home always has enough qualified, trained and awake staff to protect residents' health, safety and welfare and to evacuate every resident within three minutes, and that coverage is planned in advance and recorded.
policies.policy: This policy meets 82-13-1-.05(8)(j) (proposed), which requires a statement of what constitutes the staffing requirements and how the residence will ensure that staff are trained, and 82-13-1-.09(5) (proposed), which requires a monthly plan for specific staff coverage in advance of the month, a record of actual staff coverage, and a plan for provision of all required services. The training element of .05(8)(j) is carried out under STF-04 (orientation, training, competency) and STF-05 (employee health); the credential element is in STF-03 and the oversight and assignment of duties element is in STF-02. [AGENCY NAME] keeps enough qualified, trained staff on duty at all times to protect residents. The staffing ratio is set so that all residents can be evacuated within three minutes. The proposed rule sets no numeric ratio, so [AGENCY NAME] sets the minimum for each home in its program description based on residents' ISPs, observation levels (OBS-01) and drill results (EMG-03). Staff must be awake in the home at all times during their scheduled shift. DBHDD describes awake staff as a longstanding expectation tied to the Medicaid State Plan rate methodology, which assumes 24-hour awake staff. Staff may not use the home as a personal residence. Residents may be in the home without staff only when the ISP documents their assessed capacity to be independent. Residents are not staff and may not be required to do staff tasks unless the ISP documents voluntary participation. [AGENCY NAME] pays staff in line with the Fair Labor Standards Act (29 CFR 552). The proposed Chapter 82-13-1 is still in rulemaking. [AGENCY NAME] follows the requirements as written here and will update this policy when the rules are final (GOV-04).

definitions.definition: A staff member who is alert, on their feet or otherwise actively on duty, and physically present in the home for the whole scheduled shift. Sleeping on duty is not permitted.
The written schedule, made before the month begins, that names the staff assigned to every shift in each home, back-up staff, and who provides each required service.
The daily record of who actually worked each shift, with times in and out and any changes from the plan.
The requirement that staffing on every shift be enough to move all residents to safety within three minutes.
Services residents need each day under their ISP and this manual, such as medication supervision, personal care, meals, transportation, appointments, community activities and supervision.

procedures: The Administrator sets the minimum number of awake staff for each shift in each home. This is based on resident ISPs, assessed level of observation (OBS-01), medical and behavior needs, home layout, and results of timed evacuation drills. The minimum is written in the program description and the coverage plan.

At every fire drill (EMG-03), the staff member in charge records the time taken to evacuate all residents. If it exceeds three minutes, the Administrator adds staff or changes the evacuation plan within 1 business day and repeats the drill.

By the 20th of each month, the Administrator or Responsible Staff Person prepares and signs the coverage plan for the next month. It lists each shift, the named staff, back-up staff, which staff are trained in BCLS, first aid and medication supervision, and who will provide each required service.

The coverage plan includes a written plan for required services: medication passes, meals, personal care, transportation, appointments and community activities. Each service has a named person assigned for each shift.
The coverage plan is posted in the home's staff area and given to each scheduled employee. Changes are made in writing, initialed and dated by the Administrator or Responsible Staff Person.

Staff sign in and out at the beginning and end of every shift. The shift supervisor records the actual coverage the same day, including names, hours worked and any difference from the plan. This is the record of actual coverage.

Staff must stay awake and attentive for the entire shift. Staff may not sleep, may not rest in a bedroom, and may not leave the home unless another qualified staff member has taken over. At shift change the outgoing staff member remains until the incoming staff member arrives and receives a verbal and written report.

If a staff member cannot work a shift, they call [PHONE] as early as possible and no later than [NUMBER OF HOURS] hours before the shift. The Responsible Staff Person fills the shift from the on-call or back-up list. No home is ever left without the required awake staff, and the Administrator or Responsible Staff Person covers directly if needed.

Residents are left without staff only if the resident's ISP states their assessed capacity to be independent, how long and when, conditions, emergency steps and how to reach staff. The ISP team reviews the assessment at each ISP review and after any incident or change in condition. Staff follow the ISP exactly, and no resident is left alone without this documentation.

Staff may not live in the home, and may not stay overnight when off duty. Off-duty staff and guests may not stay in the home. The Administrator checks for compliance during monthly supervisory visits.

Residents are never counted in staffing and are not asked to do staff tasks, such as supervising other residents or doing the home's required cleaning, laundry or cooking for others. A resident may help voluntarily only if the ISP documents that the resident chose it, what the activity is, and that they may stop at any time (RGT-01).

No new employee is counted in coverage or works alone with residents until all minimum training and documented competence are complete (STF-04). Employees in training may shadow shifts, but they do not count toward the staffing minimum.
Only employees age 18 or older are scheduled, and the Administrator must be at least 21. The Administrator confirms age when staff are hired (STF-03).

[AGENCY NAME] pays all direct-care staff for every hour worked, including overtime, in line with the Fair Labor Standards Act (29 CFR 552). Because staff are awake and on duty for the whole shift, all shift hours are counted as hours worked. [AGENCY NAME] does not rely on a companionship or live-in exemption. A supervisor reviews and signs off timesheets each pay period (GOV-03).

Each month the Administrator compares the actual coverage record with the plan. Missed shifts, late arrivals, shifts covered by overtime and any shortage are listed and sent to the QI committee (QA-01). The Administrator corrects patterns by changing schedules or hiring.

When a resident is admitted or has a change of condition, the Administrator and nurse decide whether staffing must increase before the admission or change takes effect (ADM-01, HLT-03). Staffing changes are recorded in the coverage plan.
The Administrator keeps coverage plans, actual coverage records, timesheets and ISP independence assessments for the retention period in REC-01.

responsibilities.duty: Sets minimum staffing, approves monthly coverage plans, reviews actual coverage, ensures budget for adequate staffing and ensures compliance with wage and hour requirements.
Fills open shifts, makes sure required awake staff are on duty and the required services are provided, and keeps coverage records current.
Arrive on time, stay awake and in the home for the full shift, sign in and out, follow the coverage plan and report any shortage immediately.
Assesses and documents any resident's capacity to be independent without staff, and reviews it regularly.
Includes coverage variances and evacuation times in the quarterly QI review.

documentation: Monthly staff coverage plans (made before each month)
Daily record of actual staff coverage, sign-in/out sheets and timesheets with supervisory sign-off
Written plan for provision of all required services
Evacuation drill times (EMG-03)
ISP documentation of assessed capacity to be independent, where applicable
ISP documentation of voluntary resident participation in household tasks, where applicable
Monthly coverage variance review and corrective actions
On-call and back-up staff list

policies.category: Staffing, staff training and credential verification
policies.title: Professional Oversight and Assignment of Duties
policies.applies_to: Governing Body, Administrator, Developmental Disabilities Professional (DDP), nursing and clinical professionals, supervisors, and all staff
policies.purpose: To make sure that appropriate professionals oversee resident services and that every employee is assigned only duties that fit their position, training and experience and respect residents' rights.
policies.policy: This policy meets 82-13-1-.05(8)(j)1 (proposed). Appropriate professional staff oversee the services, support, care and treatment provided, including reviewing clinical documentation, conducting assessments, developing behavior support plans, service plans, healthcare plans and other protocols, and carrying out assessment, care and treatment activities as defined in the professional practice acts. This policy also meets 82-13-1-.05(8)(j)3 (proposed). Personnel are assigned duties consistent with their position, training and experience and with the requirements of Section .15 of the proposed rules (residents' rights). [AGENCY NAME] employs or contracts at least one Developmental Disabilities Professional (DDP). All nursing delivered under the CLA license is provided by nurses with site-specific nursing enrollment who meet the NOW/COMP contracting requirements in Parts II and III of the DBHDD Provider Manual. Tasks that require a license, such as nursing assessments, delegation, or clinical assessments, are done only by people licensed to perform them. Every employee has a written job description, and a supervisor signs off on service notes and timesheets. Residents are not used as staff and may not be required to perform staff tasks unless the ISP documents voluntary participation (STF-01).

definitions.definition: A professional who meets the qualifications for a DDP in the DBHDD Provider Manual and oversees service planning and quality of services for people with intellectual and developmental disabilities.

Staff who hold the license, certification or degree required by their professional practice act or by DBHDD for the task, such as a registered nurse, licensed practical nurse, licensed clinician or DDP.
The enrollment required for nursing services delivered at a specific CLA site, which must meet the NOW/COMP Part II and Part III contracting requirements.
A licensed nurse's assignment of a task to a trained, competent unlicensed staff member, within what the Georgia Nurse Practice Act allows, with the nurse retaining responsibility for oversight.

procedures: The Governing Body names the DDP in writing and records the DDP's name, qualifications, start date and coverage plan in the personnel file and the organization chart. If the DDP leaves, the Administrator tells the Governing Body within 1 business day and fills the role within [NUMBER] days using an interim qualified DDP.

The Administrator maintains an organization chart and written job descriptions for every position, including Administrator, Responsible Staff Person, DDP, nurse, direct support professional and any contracted professional. Each description lists qualifications, duties, supervisor and required training. Employees sign their job description at hire and when it changes.

Before each nurse begins service, the Administrator confirms the nurse's license and the site-specific nursing enrollment for this CLA site, and confirms that NOW/COMP Part II and III contracting requirements are met (see HLT-01, STF-03). No nursing service is provided or billed under this license without that enrollment.

The DDP or other qualified professional reviews each resident's clinical and service documentation at least monthly, including ISP progress, service notes, incident reports and behavior data. The reviewer signs and dates the review and writes any follow-up needed.

Assessments are done only by qualified professionals. A licensed nurse does the health assessments and healthcare plans, a qualified clinician does behavior assessments and behavior support plans (RST-02), and the ISP team does person-centered planning (PCS-01).

A licensed nurse delegates tasks to unlicensed staff only when the Nurse Practice Act allows it and after the staff member has been trained and found competent in writing (MED-04, STF-04). The nurse stays responsible for oversight and re-evaluates the delegation when the resident's condition changes.

Staff are assigned only tasks consistent with their position, training and experience. Before assigning a new task, the supervisor checks the personnel file to verify that the training and competency validation for that task are documented.

Staff are not assigned any duty that conflicts with residents' rights in the proposed rules or in this manual. Examples are managing residents' money without the safeguards in RGT-03, using restrictive interventions outside RST-01, or restricting access to visitors, food or the community (RGT-01).

Residents are not used as staff. The Administrator reviews the home each month for any resident doing staff work. If a resident wants to help with home tasks, the ISP documents the choice, the task, that participation is voluntary and that the resident may stop at any time.

Each employee has a supervisor. The supervisor reviews and signs service notes and timesheets each pay period before payroll, checks that notes match the ISP and shifts worked, and returns incomplete notes to the author for correction within 2 business days (GOV-03).

The Administrator or Responsible Staff Person observes each direct-care employee at work at least [NUMBER] times per quarter and records the observation, with feedback. Concerns are handled under STF-07.

Every year, the supervisor reviews each employee's job description, performance evaluation and training record to confirm duties still match the employee's position, training and experience (STF-04). Changes in duties are recorded.

The Administrator reports to the Governing Body each quarter on the professional oversight in place, DDP coverage, nursing enrollment status and any assignment concerns. Contracted providers are included in the quarterly report (QA-02).

The Administrator keeps job descriptions, the organization chart, DDP designation, nursing enrollment records, delegation records, oversight reviews and supervisory sign-offs in the administrative and personnel files.

responsibilities.duty: Designates the DDP, approves the organization chart and ensures that professional oversight is in place.
Assigns duties, keeps job descriptions, confirms licenses and nursing enrollment, and ensures supervisory review is done.
Provides professional oversight of services, reviews clinical documentation and participates in assessments and plans.
Conducts health assessments, develops healthcare plans, delegates tasks within the practice act and oversees health care.
Review and sign off service notes and timesheets and observe staff performance.
Perform only duties they are trained and assigned for and report any assignment outside their training.

documentation: Organization chart and signed job descriptions
DDP designation and qualifications
Nursing licenses and site-specific nursing enrollment records
Monthly professional review of clinical documentation
Delegation and competency records
Supervisory sign-off on service notes and timesheets
Supervisory observation records and annual duty review
Quarterly oversight report to the Governing Body

policies.category: Staffing, staff training and credential verification
policies.title: Credential Verification, Registry and Background Checks
policies.applies_to: Administrator, hiring staff, all applicants and employees, and contracted professionals
policies.purpose: To make sure that every person who works or may work with residents is screened before employment, that licenses, credentials, experience and competence are verified, and that no one who is disqualified or unqualified has contact with residents.
policies.policy: This policy meets 82-13-1-.05(8)(j)2 (proposed): procedures for verifying licenses, credentials, experience and competence of staff. [AGENCY NAME] completes a registry check, a records check application and a criminal background check before employment for every person who will work in the home, including a potential administrator (O.C.G.A. 37-1-141 and 37-1-143). An eligible criminal background determination is kept in each personnel file. [AGENCY NAME] also completes a criminal records check under DBHDD Policy 04-104 and a motor vehicle record (MVR) check before hire. The Administrator verifies a five-year employment history for each CLA staff member. Professional licenses and credentials are verified with the issuing authority, and experience and competence are verified before duties are assigned. The Administrator must be at least 21 years old and every employee at least 18. No one begins work, orientation involving resident contact or direct contact with residents until the required checks are complete and eligible. The proposed Chapter 82-13-1 is still in rulemaking, and [AGENCY NAME] follows the requirements as written here and will update this policy when the rules are final (GOV-04).

definitions.definition: The check of the registry required before employment by the CLA rules and O.C.G.A. 37-1-141 and 37-1-143.
The application submitted before employment to obtain the records check required by O.C.G.A. 37-1-141 and 37-1-143.
A written determination that the person's criminal background check makes them eligible for employment, kept in the personnel file.
Motor vehicle record, the driving history obtained from the state for each employee.
Verification of a license or credential directly with the issuing board or institution, not only from a copy supplied by the applicant.

procedures: Before making an offer, the Administrator or designee gives each applicant the application. It lists the last five years of employment, education, licenses, certifications and references, and asks about any criminal history. The applicant signs to authorize checks. [AGENCY NAME] does not hire anyone under 18, and the Administrator must be at least 21. Age is verified from a government-issued photo ID.

Before the person's first day of employment, the Administrator submits the registry check, the records check application and the criminal background check as required by O.C.G.A. 37-1-141 and 37-1-143. This applies to every person who will work in the home and to a potential administrator. The date submitted and the results are recorded.

The Administrator also completes the criminal records check required by DBHDD Policy 04-104 and records the result. A person is not placed in the schedule, in orientation with resident contact or in a home until an eligible determination is received and filed. If the result is not eligible or is pending, the person does not work.

If the check shows a criminal history, a registry listing or an unclear result, the Administrator does not employ the person until the matter is resolved under the applicable rule and Policy 04-104. The Administrator documents the decision and the reasons in a confidential file.

The Administrator obtains the applicant's MVR before hire. A person who will drive residents must have a valid Georgia or otherwise valid driver's license and an MVR that meets the standard in ENV-02. A person whose MVR does not meet the standard is not assigned to drive. The MVR is filed in the personnel file.

The Administrator verifies the five-year employment history personally by contacting past employers by phone or in writing. Each contact is recorded with date, person spoken to, dates of employment and any concerns. Gaps are explained by the applicant in writing. The Administrator signs and dates the verification.
At least two references are contacted, and at least one must be from a current or recent employer or a professional contact. Reference responses are written and filed.

For every position that requires a license, certification or degree (such as a nurse, DDP or clinician), the Administrator verifies it directly with the issuing board or institution before the person starts. The printout or confirmation is dated and filed. The Administrator confirms the license is active, unrestricted and not expired.
For nursing staff, the Administrator also confirms the site-specific nursing enrollment for this CLA site (STF-02) before any nursing service is provided.

The Administrator confirms the experience and competence the position requires by reviewing resume, interviews and reference feedback. For direct-care staff, the supervisor confirms that the applicant can read and follow written instructions, can communicate with residents and understands the duties. Documented competence in required skills is confirmed after training (STF-04).

As a Medicaid-enrolled provider, [AGENCY NAME] also confirms before hire and at the intervals required by its Medicaid agreements that the person is not excluded from federal health care programs (GOV-03).

For each person, the Administrator completes a pre-employment checklist showing every check, the date requested, the date received and the result. The Administrator signs it before the person is added to the schedule.

The Administrator rechecks licenses and credentials at each expiration date, and rechecks MVRs and background checks as required by DBHDD policy. The Administrator keeps a tracking calendar of expiration dates and reviews it monthly.

Employees must tell the Administrator within 1 business day if they are arrested or charged with any offense, or if their license or driving privileges are suspended, restricted or revoked. The Administrator reviews the facts right away and may remove the person from resident contact while the matter is reviewed.
Contracted professionals and volunteers who will have unsupervised contact with residents go through the same checks before they begin.
Background check results and similar sensitive records are kept in a secure file as set out in CONF-01 and STF-06.

responsibilities.duty: Completes or oversees all checks and verifications, verifies five-year employment history, decides eligibility, and keeps the tracking calendar.
Collect applications and consents and do not schedule anyone until the Administrator confirms clearance.
Ensures hiring of an Administrator follows these checks, including the pre-employment checks of a potential administrator.
Provide accurate information and report arrests, charges, and license or driving changes within 1 business day.

documentation: Signed employment application with five-year employment history
Registry check, records check application and criminal background check results
Eligible criminal background determination
Criminal records check under DBHDD Policy 04-104
MVR
Employment and reference verification notes
License and credential verification printouts and expiration tracking calendar
Proof of age
Pre-employment checklist signed by the Administrator

policies.category: Staffing, staff training and credential verification
policies.title: Orientation, Training and Competency
policies.applies_to: Administrator, supervisors, trainers, and all employees and contractors with resident contact
policies.purpose: To make sure every employee is oriented before contacting residents, completes all required training, shows competence before working alone, and keeps skills current through annual training and evaluation.
policies.policy: This policy meets 290-9-37-.07(3)(k) (current codified rule), how the residence will ensure that staff are trained, and the matching proposed rule 82-13-1-.05(8)(j) (proposed). No employee works alone with residents until all minimum training and documented competence are complete. Every employee completes orientation before any direct contact with residents. Orientation covers HIPAA, residents' rights, mandatory abuse, neglect and exploitation reporting, and the HCBS Settings Rule. Within 60 days of hire, non-designated staff complete the full training list. Every employee completes at least 16 hours of training each year, has annual competency validation and receives an annual performance evaluation. Staff hold current first aid and BCLS training and recertify on time, and at least one staff member trained in BCLS and first aid is on duty every shift in this 24-hour residential setting. HIPAA training is provided to the workforce as required by 45 CFR 164.530(b). Training and competency evidence is kept in the personnel file. The proposed Chapter 82-13-1 is still in rulemaking, and [AGENCY NAME] follows the current rule and the DBHDD Provider Manual and will update this policy when the rules are final (GOV-04).

definitions.definition: Required training completed before any direct contact with residents, covering HIPAA, rights, mandatory ABE reporting and the HCBS Settings Rule.
Documented observation or testing by a qualified trainer or supervisor showing that an employee can perform a task correctly and safely.
Basic cardiac life support, a course with a hands-on skills test, from a nationally recognized provider.
At least 16 hours of training each year in job-related topics, documented with date, topic, hours and trainer.
Staff who are not designated as professionals under the DBHDD Provider Manual. They complete the full training list within 60 days of hire.

procedures: The Administrator keeps a written training curriculum that lists orientation topics, the full required training list, the trainer, hours, method of competency validation and refresher schedule. The Administrator reviews it every year and when rules or policies change.

On or before the first day, and before any direct contact with residents, each new employee completes orientation covering: HIPAA and confidentiality (CONF-01), resident rights (RGT-01), mandatory reporting of abuse, neglect and exploitation (ABE-01), the HCBS Settings Rule (RGT-01), the code of conduct (COC-01) and the emergency plan (EMG-01).

The trainer records the orientation date, topics, trainer and the employee's signature. The employee takes a short written or oral check after the ABE reporting and rights modules. Anyone who does not pass repeats the module before contact with residents.

Before working alone with residents, each employee must complete all minimum training and have documented competence in: each resident's ISP and health plan (PCS-01, HLT-01); medication supervision, if assigned (MED-01 to MED-04); first aid and BCLS; fire safety and evacuation (EMG-03); infection control (INF-01); behavior support and restrictive intervention limits (RST-01, RST-02); health monitoring, seizures and choking (HLT-02); and the individual needs of each resident.

New employees work alongside a trained, experienced employee for [NUMBER] shifts. The trainer observes and records each competency on a checklist. Shadow shifts do not count toward the staffing minimum (STF-01). The employee is not scheduled to work alone until the Administrator or supervisor signs the competency checklist.

Within 60 days of hire, each employee completes the full training list in the curriculum, and the Administrator verifies this against the personnel file. An employee who has not finished within 60 days is not scheduled to work alone and has a written completion plan.

Every employee holds current first aid and BCLS certification before working alone, and recertifies before expiration. The Administrator tracks expiration dates and makes sure that at least one staff member trained in BCLS and first aid is on duty on every shift in each home. Coverage plans show this person (STF-01).

Each employee completes at least 16 hours of training every year, with the year counted from the hire date or the calendar year as set in the curriculum. The employee signs each session sheet, and the Administrator tallies hours by employee each quarter.

New or changed resident needs trigger additional training before an employee works with that resident. Examples are a new diagnosis, a new medication route, a new behavior support plan, a new diet or a new device. The nurse or qualified professional trains the staff and records competence.

At least once a year, a supervisor or qualified trainer validates each employee's competency by observation or return demonstration in medication supervision (where assigned), first aid and BCLS skills, emergency response, resident rights and person-centered support. The validation is signed and dated.

Each employee receives a written performance evaluation at least once a year. It reviews job performance, attendance, documentation, rights and conduct, training status and goals. The employee and supervisor sign it and the employee may add comments.
Employees who fail a competency check are retrained and re-validated. They are not assigned that task until competence is documented, and the supervisor notes the retraining plan.

Records of HIPAA training for all workforce members are kept as the HIPAA privacy rule requires (45 CFR 164.530(b)). The Administrator retrains when policies change or when a confidentiality breach shows a need (CONF-01).

The Administrator reviews training completion monthly using a tracking matrix showing each employee's orientation date, 60-day completion, BCLS and first aid expiration, annual hours, competency date and evaluation date. Overdue items are reported to the Governing Body each quarter and to QI (QA-01).
Contracted staff and any volunteer with resident contact are held to the same orientation and competency requirements for the tasks they perform.
All training sign-in sheets, certificates, competency checklists and evaluations are filed in the personnel file (STF-06).

responsibilities.duty: Maintains the curriculum, ensures orientation and training are completed on time, verifies competence and tracks the matrix.
Deliver training and validate competence in their areas and sign the competency records.
Observe staff, validate annual competency, complete evaluations and do not schedule staff to work alone before competence is documented.
Confirms that a BCLS and first aid trained employee is on every shift.
Attend and complete training, maintain certifications, and tell the supervisor before certifications expire.

documentation: Written training curriculum
Signed orientation records showing completion before direct contact
Competency checklists signed by trainer and supervisor
60-day full training list completion record
First aid and BCLS certificates with expiration dates
Annual training hour log (at least 16 hours)
Annual competency validation and performance evaluation
Training tracking matrix and quarterly report
HIPAA training records

policies.category: Staffing, staff training and credential verification
policies.title: Employee Health, TB Screening and Fitness for Duty
policies.applies_to: Administrator, nurse, supervisors, and all employees with resident contact
policies.purpose: To protect residents and staff from communicable disease and from impaired staff, by requiring tuberculosis screening, bloodborne pathogen protection and fitness for duty.
policies.policy: This policy meets the employee health and fitness portion of 82-13-1-.05(8)(j) (proposed), which requires a statement of what constitutes the staffing requirements and how the residence will ensure that staff are trained. Staff health requirements are part of the staffing requirements and protect residents. Each employee completes tuberculosis (TB) screening on hire, consisting of a risk assessment, symptom evaluation and TB test, and repeats screening after a known exposure. Screening records are kept in the personnel file. Employees must be free of illegal drugs and alcohol and of legal substances that impair the performance of their duties. [AGENCY NAME] offers bloodborne pathogen training and hepatitis B vaccination in line with the OSHA Bloodborne Pathogens Standard (29 CFR 1910.1030). The proposed Chapter 82-13-1 is still in rulemaking, and [AGENCY NAME] follows the current Provider Manual and the requirements as written here and will update this policy when the rules are final (GOV-04).

definitions.definition: The three-part process of a TB risk assessment, a symptom evaluation and a TB test (skin test or blood test), reviewed by a licensed health care professional.
Contact with a person who has been diagnosed with active TB, or who is reported by the health department or a clinician as having active TB.
A prescription or over-the-counter medication, or other legal substance, that affects an employee's alertness, judgment or physical ability to do the job safely.
Reasonably anticipated contact with blood or other potentially infectious material while doing the job.
Being physically and mentally able to do assigned duties safely, free of impairment from alcohol, illegal drugs or legal substances.

procedures: Before the first day with resident contact, each new employee completes the TB risk assessment and symptom evaluation using the form in the personnel packet. The nurse or a licensed health care professional reviews it and signs.

Before or within the time set by the nurse and no later than the start of resident contact, each employee has a TB test (a skin test or a blood test) given and read by a licensed health care professional. The result, date and reader are recorded. A person whose result is not yet available is not placed in resident contact unless the nurse documents that the risk assessment and symptom evaluation are negative and the test is scheduled within [NUMBER] days.

An employee with a positive TB test, or symptoms such as a cough lasting 3 weeks or longer, fever, night sweats, weight loss or bloody sputum, is sent for medical evaluation. The employee does not work with residents until a licensed health care provider provides written clearance. The nurse notifies the local health department as required by law.

When an employee, resident or visitor is identified as having active TB, the Administrator and nurse identify exposed employees and residents within 1 business day, coordinate with the health department, and repeat TB screening for each exposed employee as the health department and nurse direct. Results are filed.

The Administrator files TB screening records in the personnel file (STF-06), with confidential health information kept separate from other personnel records and shared only on a need-to-know basis (CONF-01).

Within 10 working days of the initial assignment and at no cost to the employee, [AGENCY NAME] offers the hepatitis B vaccine series to every employee with possible occupational exposure. An employee who declines signs the declination form and may change their mind and receive the vaccine later.

At hire and every year, employees complete bloodborne pathogen training that covers the written exposure control plan, standard precautions, personal protective equipment, handwashing, sharps handling, cleaning of blood spills, hepatitis B vaccination, and what to do after an exposure (INF-01). The trainer and the date are recorded.
[AGENCY NAME] keeps personal protective equipment such as gloves, gowns and face protection available in each home at no cost to employees, and checks supplies at least weekly.

After an exposure incident, the employee washes the area, tells the supervisor and nurse at once, and is offered a confidential medical evaluation and follow-up at no cost. The Administrator records the incident without naming the source person in unprotected records and reports it as required (ABE-02).
